speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as most members of the House know, Ethiopia is again close to facing another brutal famine. Already people are dying by the hundreds, and it is anticipated people will die by the thousands.
We are pleased to hear that Canada has agreed to provide additional moneys for food aid, but time is running out and the food is not yet reaching those in need. The international press reports of desperate conditions and significant change in the Ethiopian situation. Many people wonder how many years of famine are going to continue in Ethiopia before the situation changes.
At this time the solution is not only that of food aid, but that of politics. The Government of Canada must offer its good offices and reputation to help the people of Ethiopia come to terms with the fact that the country is no longer governed as it was in the first famine. The government has lost legitimacy and the rebels in the two provinces are now significant actors. It will take not only food aid but a major role in the Security Council and other international institutions for Canada to help with a solution.
We plead with the government to take a more active role in helping the people of Ethiopia and encouraging the international community to get more involved.

Mr. Speaker, an Environics poll carried out for the Department of Transport shows that people living in the greater Toronto area are two to one in favour of adding additional runways at Pearson International Airport.
This is in opposition to the poll I carried out in my riding last summer which showed that residents directly affected by the airport are almost two to one against expansion.
Out of 2,168 people polled, almost double the number polled by Environics, 37.4 per cent were in favour, 2 per cent were undecided, and 60.6 per cent were against.
I believe the apparent discrepancy in these two surveys can be attributed to the fact that those people polled by Environics are not people who live within the same proximity to the airport as the residents of my own riding of Brampton-Malton.
If we are to determine the effects of expansion on surrounding communities then we must ask those people who will be profoundly affected by expansion. Distortion of this important fact is not acceptable.

Mr. Speaker, last week's election in Nicaragua was a democratic event that owes its existence to the Sandinista revolution. We can be assured that, had the American backed Somoza never been overthrown, democracy would still be a stranger to Nicaragua. So would literacy, community health care, land reform and the absence of death squads, to name a few of the benefits brought on by the Sandinistas.
Nevertheless, the people of Nicaragua cried uncle under the combined burden of the trade embargo, mistakes made by the Sandinistas themselves, and the prospect of continued war with the Contras, given the

March 7, 1990
widespread expectation that Washington would not have been as gracious as Ortega if its side had lost the election.
We must hope now that Mrs. Chamorro and Daniel Ortega will be able to build an understanding based on their once mutually shared abhorrence of pre-revolutionary Nicaragua. There can be no return to those days. Essential to preventing this is the total and immediate disbanding of the Contras, something that only Washington can ensure by cutting off the Contra support and in doing so showing its respect for the views of both Chamorro and Ortega.
This having been done, negotiations about the army in Nicaragua and other issues could proceed. In the meantime, the Canadian government should continue to keep Nicaragua an important country in its development aid programs and urge President Bush to do the right thing.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to report to the House that the Town Council of Outremont has made its position clear on the language question. The resolution passed at the public meeting on March 5 this year sets forth the town's present policy and its intention to continue to provide services in English, as necessary and appropriate, to its English-speaking minority.
I may add that the resolution passed by the council is practically identical to a resolution passed in English by the Municipal Council of Elliot Lake.
I join the Mayor of the Town of Outremont in expressing the wish that the resolution will be well received by the community in general and its individual members. This resolution demonstrates, above all that economic excuses often hide serious psycho-social deficiencies with respect to human values. Bigotry and racism all too often go hand in hand.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my concern over the fiasco of low level flights in Labrador.
As associate critic for northern affairs, it is my position that we should be striving for a responsible development of our northern regions. However, this government has failed to consult Innu and Inuit Canadians properly before taking this decision to bid for a NATO training base and increase the number of low level flights in the region.
The present government seems to be falling into the habit of creating commissions to study the impact of its decisions after the fact. It did this with VIA Rail as well as with the environmental assessment of low level flights in Labrador. These actions epitomize the classic syndrome of putting the cart before the horse. Proper and comprehensive consultation must occur before decisions are implemented.
The attitude that "the sound of jets is the sound of money" only exemplifies the short-sighted approach that we should be trying to get away from.
It seems somewhat regressive that we would be creating the world's biggest battlefield in this era of closer relations and increased co-operation between east and west. Moreover, the increase of flight activity coupled with the sonic boom effect would endanger the wildlife and infringe upon the lifestyles of the thousands of people who inhabit the region and indeed would disrupt the delicate balance of the environment.

Mr. Speaker, Edmonton was host to the great debate last Monday. It was sponsored by the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce as part of its debt reduction conference.
I would like to thank the Edmonton chamber for sponsoring the conference. They studied the debt situa-
March 7, 1990

tion in a responsible manner and came up with some thoughtful solutions. We all know who won the debate. I can quote CJCA panellist, Professor Tom Powrie, who said: "Michael Wilson won hands down".
Or perhaps I should quote David Bailey, the editor in chief of the Edmonton Sun who bluntly said: "Doug Young lost it".
The Edmonton Journal columnist Mark Lisac thoughtfully remarked: "Spectators saw Liberal finance critic, Doug Young, take on one of the real heavyweights in Canadian politics and get pounded into impudence."
Albertans love blood sports. Let's do it again.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to welcome you and all Canadians to what will become a regular feature on Wednesdays. The NDP will present the corporate welfare bum of the week. Each week we will choose one winner from three nominees of large corporations that have not paid their fair share of taxes.
The nominees are Bramalea Limited. This property company did not pay any taxes from 1984 to 1988. Its net income increased in that period from $11.2 million to $41.2 million, but still no taxes paid.
The second nominee is another property company, Trizec Corporation which paid only $600,000 in taxes both in 1987 and 1988. Its net income for 1987 was $101 million. In 1988 it was $90 million.
Our final nominee is Hees International which, you guessed it, did not pay a penny in taxes from 1981 to 1987.
Now, for our winner-the envelope, please: The winner of corporate welfare bum of the week, Elees International.
The judges felt that this financial and management services company deserves the title as it seems to do little else than own other companies. Not to worry if our other two companies might feel slighted, Hees owns them-

speechtext:

Oral Questions FISHERIES

Mr. Speaker, Canada recently reached an agreement with the United States on the implementation of the free trade panel report on the export of unprocessed British Columbia salmon and herring. Under the agreement U.S. processors now have the right to buy, if they choose, up to 20 per cent of B.C. unprocessed salmon and herring this year and up to 25 per cent over the next three years.
Of this agreement, UBC professor Dr. Peter Pearse, who headed a royal commission into the B.C. fishery in 1981-82, said: "No foreigner is going to be able to take west coast fish unless they have been caught by a Canadian and a Canadian fisherman chooses to sell them. Last year, under the then existing rules, Canadian processors purchased more American fish for processing in Canada than vice versa.
All the evidence is that free trade in raw fish creates more jobs in Canada, not less. The Canadian fishing industry has shown it can compete on the world market and it is up to them to remain competitive".
With the combination of continued government management of the resource and private initiative to process and market the resource, the fisheries will remain strong and viable for the benefit of all British Columbians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister.
When the Premier of Saskatchewan spoke on television earlier this week, he said:
When the federal budget was introduced, additional pressures were put on our province. The immediate effect was a drop of $33 million in transfer payments from the federal government. Over the long term, an annual shortfall of about $100 million will occur at a time when the people of Saskatchewan can least afford it.
The premier went on to say that the budget, in combination with the Americans stealing our traditional wheat markets, and I quote: "amounts to the world declaring economic war on Saskatchewan".

March 7, 1990
Oral Questions
Will the government listen to the Premier of Saskatchewan, declare a ceasefire in its economic war with Saskatchewan and the other provinces, and withdraw its misguided budget?

Mr. Speaker, surely the hon. member understands that there is no economic war, using his terms, when we are transferring to the provinces $34 billion next year. We are increasing those transfers by 3 per cent, which is the same as the increase in the federal government programs.
We are asking the provinces to share in this national problem of getting the deficit down. We must ask them to do that because of the size of those transfer payments. They represent about one-third of our program spending. We are asking them to be a one-third part of our expenditure control program. I think that it is only fair what we are doing.
He talked about the problems with international subsidy wars. My colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, has commented on those on many occasions. We are doing what we can, in international fora, in the trade negotiations and in the summit discussions where the Prime Minister has represented us. In many, many ways we are dealing with this international subsidy war problem.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I spoke of an economic war with Saskatchewan waged by this government, the term "economic war" was used by Premier Devine, a Conservative premier, in a speech on television. If the minister has any concerns about those words, he should take them up with Premier Devine.
In his speech, Mr. Devine also said:
I told the Deputy Prime Minister Saskatchewan people need a half a billion dollars right now to get ready for the spring seeding, and another $400 million just to compete with the unfair subsidies of foreign governments. I also told Mr. Mazankowski Canada needs a billion dollar contingency fund to keep us from becoming casualties in subsidy wars.
What specific answer will the government give to this plea for help from Saskatchewan, or will the minister just have to admit that the government still has no plans to help the farmers of Saskatchewan and the farmers across this country?

As I indicated to the House yesterday-

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Mr. Devine made his speech two days ago, but for the past two months it has been public knowledge that the Atlantic fisheries are in trouble, and the government has had plenty of time to organize a recovery program.
Mr. Speaker, although the Prime Minister was in Halifax yesterday, he failed to take this opportunity to announce a fisheries recovery program for the region.
March 7, 1990

Why didn't the Prime Minister announce a recovery program yesterday for the region's fishermen and processing plants?
This crisis has gone on far too long. When are we going to see this government come up with a real action plan?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that if the hon. leader of the Opposition would care to recall this country's recent history with respect to fisheries, he would realize the Liberal Party is hardly in a position to tell us what to do since it is responsible for everything that led up to what has now become the Atlantic fisheries crisis.
The Prime Minister has refused and this government refuses-
Oh, oh!
They don't like the answer. They ask intelligent questions, but they don't want an answer!
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the new Fisheries Minister, and I want to take this opportunity to wish him every success in his new post.
Hear, hear!

There has been a lot of talk about special assistance programs for communities affected by the Atlantic fisheries crisis.
The Prime Minister and other ministers have referred in very general terms to generous programs involving billions of dollars. The minister himself said last week that the Prime Minister had not made any promises. Last night, however, when faced with unruly demonstrators, the Prime Minister repeated his vague promises.
Is the new minister at liberty to tell us whether there will be a special aid program with additional funding, or is he going to give us more of the same and blame it all on somebody else, as he did just now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the communities I visited last week and the groups I spoke to do not consider the $130 million the government gave to these communities a few months ago to be a "rehash".
Oral Questions
I can tell the hon. member that in my consultations last week, and not to my surprise since I know Atlantic Canadians, not one group asked me or asked the government to throw money at the problem.
We have a serious situation in the Atlantic region. The government has already given a preliminary response. We must consider the Harris report; we must also consider how in the future we can best avoid a situation like the one we are now going through.
Furthermore, in recent months, the government has put in place mechanisms to come up with these solutions. And if the hon. member wants to know if action will be taken, the answer is yes. Measures will be announced as soon as they have been decided.

Mr. Speaker, it is still a "rehash" and what is more, we have to wait for it.

In the case of fishing communities that are losing their whole base of support when large companies decide to pack up and leave, will the minister exercise his authority and prevent the companies from transferring their boats and licences to other ports, so that these communities can continue to live from the sea and still be there when the stocks return to normal? Will he exercise his authority?
Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): Mr. Speaker, I am quite amazed at the member referring only to the people affected by those announced plant closures.
Of course we are not talking about the thousands of employees who are already working in other plants that do function.
Where?
In Lunenburg and other areas of Atlantic Canada.
Only in Lunenburg.

Any quick fix for the Liberal Party; it is famous for that. I do not think that is the way the way to deal with this matter now. There is no quick fix for a serious problem.
It is all right to blame us in the House and to blame the government for the situation, but as I said in Atlantic

March 7, 1990
Oral Questions
Canada-and every premier agreed with me, including Mr. Wells, Mr. McKenna, Mr. Buchanan and Mr. Ghiz-we have to work together and be the architects of the solution together.
We win nothing by just having mud thrown at us supposedly for being responsible for a situation which developed over a long period of time. We want good solutions and that is what we are striving for.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
On December 13, 1989, the Prime Minister made a commitment to Atlantic Canadians that the government would respond to the crisis in the Atlantic fishery, and I quote, "with exactly the same kind of generosity and enthusiasm" that was shown to western farmers.
Will the Prime Minister assure Atlantic Canadians that the Atlantic Fisheries Adjustment Program that he referred to yesterday will ensure that Atlantic Canadians can remain employed in their own communities? Will he tell the House today what measures will be taken and exactly when?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend raises the question of an adjustment program, but there is more to it than that.
As the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans has just indicated, the government responded initially with a $130 million package designed to deal with the immediate hardships encountered by those in fishing communities in Atlantic Canada.
We are now in the process of preparing an important response to the Harris commission which deals with conservation and other important policy measures to ensure that the resource is no longer depleted in the future and remains an asset for Atlantic Canada.
Third, there is a dimension to it which we are going to deal with in an Atlantic Canada adjustment package particularly designed for the fishery which we hope, following the minister's discussions with various premiers, fishing leaders, union leaders and plant owners,
will bring a definitive solution for fishermen in Atlantic Canada.
What we do not want to do is repeat some of the experiences of the past which solved the problem for a brief period of time and then caused it to recur again. We want a definitive solution in the interests of the people of Atlantic Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Prime Minister.
I have to say that Atlantic Canadians need a definitive solution too, but Atlantic Canadians are now without jobs. This problem has been known for a long time. It is not a new problem and the Prime Minister knows that.
Similarly, the crisis for Canadian farmers is not a new problem and it continues to get worse. This year in Saskatchewan alone the farm income is expected to go down 101 per cent, a negative farm income.
With spring seeding around the comer, the government says it is studying the problem. Farmers cannot wait for another study. They are losing their farms now. Will the Prime Minister act immediately to implement a specific farm support program?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course it is an urgent problem and of course it is important to assess in a precise way the magnitude of the situation. Mr. Devine and other provincial governments are working together with us in doing just that.
As I indicated to the House yesterday, supplementary drought payment cheques are being distributed right at this very moment.
I want to remind the hon. member that the government's support for agriculture in the province of Saskatchewan is very great. It is very huge, as a matter of fact. For every dollar that the Saskatchewan government puts into agriculture, the federal government has put in between $10 and $12.
Now that is a pretty solid record and certainly does not say to me that the Government of Canada is avoiding the problem. It says to me that the Government of Canada is very cognizant of the problem. It has a solid track record and we are going to work with the provinces in trying to

provide the kind of solution to which the hon. member refers. I hope that we will have the support of her and her party when we bring it down. I am sure that we will.

Mr. Speaker, the minister responsible for fisheries said that this government does not want to do a quick fix. Well, farmers in the west and people in the Atlantic region are seeing no fix.
My final question to the Prime Minister is very specific. When will western farmers and Atlantic fishermen receive the long promised support programs?

Mr. Speaker, the government responded very generously to the needs of farmers across Canada in the past and we have responded as well to the fishermen. We are working, as the minister has indicated, very closely with the producing provinces which are confronted with the kinds of problems that Premier Devine has described.
I have just returned from meetings in Atlantic Canada yesterday, including-
Very friendly meetings.
Yes, very friendly meetings, apart from a few of my hon. friend's friends who were there.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish to bring to members' attention the presence in the gallery of the Hon. C. Stephen Rogers, Speaker (Designate) of the British Columbia Legislative Assembly and Mr. Mark Rose, Opposition House Leader.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, this week the Premier of Saskatchewan estimated that one-third of the farmers of Saskatchewan are facing an immediate debt crisis and an additional 20,000 farmers are worried about the possibility.
Oral Questions
Can the Minister of Agriculture tell this House today what assistance the government will provide for Canadian farmers, or is he waiting for an election to be called in Saskatchewan before he acts?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I indicated to the House yesterday and again today, we are working very closely with the provinces in trying to put together a package that will respond to the needs to which the hon. member refers. I hope that we can do that in a time that would clearly demonstrate the government's intentions, with the support of the provinces, hopefully before spring seeding.

Mr. Speaker, since January 1 export prices for wheat have dropped by $10 per tonne. Yet grain stocks are at the lowest level they have been for many years. The minister refuses to recognize that his blind belief in the free market system, that no longer exists, is destroying the family farm in Canada.
When will the minister stop acting like a bushleaguer of international trade and fight fire with fire by introducing Canadian programs to combat American and European export subsidies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am almost tempted to talk about bushleagues but I won't because this is a very serious matter.
The hon. member knows that we have responded in the past and we intend to respond now because of the impact that the price war has on the income situation of all farmers who are producing grains and oilseeds. I think the hon. member is also aware that while the subsidy war still continues it has been reduced somewhat substantially. The Europeans, for example, were subsidizing to the tune of about $200 per tonne. Today it is about $80 per tonne. The United States, under their EEP program, is subsidizing in the order of about $20 per tonne.
In fact, since 1986-87 grain prices have strengthened and we certainly do not support the kind of price war that is going on. We are doing everything that we can in our power to resolve this trade dispute through the MTN negotiations and that will certainly provide the long term solution.

March 7, 1990
Oral Questions
We have, as a government, supported the farmers on the deficiency that occurred as a result of the trade war and we are looking at that again along with the drought program, the shortfall in cash to put the crop in, and all the other things related to that to develop the kind of package which I am sure the hon. member will support.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. The chairman of the Hamilton Harbour Commission, Peter Lush, who was appointed, by the way, by the Prime Minister, is both the listing agent and owner of a real estate firm selling property which the harbour commission wants to buy.
The Commission has already purchased land from the same real estate firm of which Mr. Lush was a member when he was a member of the harbour commission. Would the Prime Minister not agree that this is a blatant conflict of interest?
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend will know that the Hamilton Harbour Commission operates at arm's length from the government.
Oh, oh!
It is financially self-sufficient. My hon. friend is-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Is that short arms or long arms?
Why, it's almost independent.
They either want to hear it or they don't.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. minister.

I do not want to dredge up any old allegations that might embarrass my friends opposite. This issue was thoroughly reviewed by the commission at the time the original allegation was made and we are satisfied that there was no conflict of interest.

Mr. Speaker, old allegations on a new member of Parliament won't cut the mustard.
The Hamilton harbour commissioners were established by an act of Parliament. That act of Parliament states quite clearly that the corporation shall not have any transactions of any pecuniary nature either in buying or selling with any members thereof directly or indirectly-
Back in 1986, Peter Lush admitted that he would not become a harbour commissioner if it meant giving up the listings his firm had. That is property, of course, that the Hamilton Harbour Commission was interested in buying.
Does the Prime Minister not agree that Mr. Lush has one of two options: He either gives up his listings or he resigns from the commission.

Mr. Speaker, if my hon. friend has any information which impacts on conflict of interest which he is prepared to give, I suggest that he give it to me. Otherwise, why doesn't he see if he has the nerve to make that same allegation outside the confines of this House.

Mr. Speaker, in a statement in Halifax yesterday the Prime Minister expressed scepticism that NATO would proceed with the Goose Bay low-level test flight facility given the reduction of tensions in eastern Europe.
My question is directed to the Prime Minister. Given widespread Canadian opposition to the facility and the disastrous impact it will have on the way of life of the Labrador Innu, will he exercise Canadian sovereignty on this issue rather than passively leaving the decision to NATO and, in the interests of the Innu and all Canadian people, cancel its bid to NATO for the low-level test facility?

Mr. Speaker, I think the NDP members will have to make up their minds. On the one hand they ask us to promote job creation in Newfoundland and Labrador. When we try to bring in thousands of jobs for the benefit of Newfoundland and Labrador, they are the first people to be opposed before it even has an opportunity to be examined carefully by the people in Newfoundland and Labrador.
March 7, 1990

The Government of Canada, as a member of NATO, was approached with a proposal which we agreed to submit to environmental review and to cabinet consideration if NATO decided to proceed.
I indicated yesterday in Halifax that in light of recent developments, I personally-not NATO but I personally-was somewhat sceptical as to whether the entire project would, in the light of these new circumstances, appear. My hon. friend cannot take yes for an answer.

It is seldom that we get yes for an answer or any answer at all from that side, Mr. Speaker.
Given the disastrous cuts to native programs in the department of the Secretary of State, would the minister not consider it advisable to create jobs in Canada and that rather than stripping native organizations of their leadership, cutting out native media altogether, eliminating the basis of native broadcasting and eliminating friendship centres, the place to create jobs would be in those programs rather than in a test flight facility that the Prime Minister himself considers obsolete and is sceptical about?
Mr. Speaker, I do not consider it obsolete at all. I did not express a view in regard to any degree of obsolescence. I simply responded-
You're obsolete.
Well, my hon. friend says I am obsolete. Hang on to your hat. In 1992 we are going to make the NDP obsolete in this country.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence.
On March 2, a Canadian Armed Forces CF-18 broke the sound barrier in the Gatineau-Hull-Aylmer area.
Can the minister tell us what regulations the Canadian Armed Forces have for CF-18 pilots concerning flights in Canada? Will you communicate with Canadian Armed
Oral Questions
Forces officials to prevent a recurrence of such an incident?

speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, this is important. The member asks a question that is important.
Aircraft shall now be flown at supersonic speeds:
a.	except in an emergency or when otherwise directed by the CDS
or an OCC;
b.	below flight level 300-

The hon. member brings this issue to our attention and I will bring to the attention of the House that the pilot in question, because of the investigation, has been grounded and appropriate action will be taken.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy. This year's energy Estimates show a $246 million cut for conservation and alternative energy. How can the minister support these cuts when this government says that a clean environment is a priority?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there were cuts made in the budget for my department in a number of areas and that is supported by me. I take responsibility for those cuts. It was necessary to do so to bring down the deficit and have the economic well-being that we need in order that energy can grow as an economic factor.
Also we have to move away from the direction of the former government, through its NEP, in that we had vestiges of the NEP. Namely, if there is a dollar to be found let's spend it because we will have energy efficiency. That is just not the way to go.

Mr. Speaker, the United States is very concerned about its deficit and it has increased spending in this area. Without continued

March 7, 1990
Oral Questions
government leadership and support we are going to lose our lead in this whole area to the United States and Europe.
Will the government stop discriminating against alternative energy through its taxing and spending and give alternative energy the priority it deserves?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I find that passing strange from that member. I was in Charlottetown a few weeks ago where the biomass project was put into place on which we spent $7 million per capita. That was one of the highest expenditures for alternate energy in Canada. I wish she would start saying thank you for those kind of things rather than the kinds of things she is saying.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Immigration and it concerns the Federal Court decision which ruled that the minister's refugee backlog system is illegal. Irrespective of whether the minister has read the court decision, she knows full well that there is much confusion over the present status of that system.
Can the minister clarify for the House whether the current backlog system is conducting business as usual, or whether she has issued directives through her officials to suspend those operations until that system is changed or abolished altogether?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the hon. member, who should not have to be reminded of this, that the judgment did not concern the whole of the backlog review system. The case challenged a single part of the backlog clearance process, which was the frontend humanitarian and compassionate criteria, the guidelines that went out.
This backlog clearance was established to deal with claims in the refugee status and the determination remains the primary issue. I want to remind him of that.
I can tell him that within the department the backlog clearance system is proceeding. The interviews are continuing to take place, but the decisions on those
interviews are being held in abeyance until we see the written reasons for the judgment.

Mr. Speaker that answer is simply incredible. If the front end is bad, what makes you think that the back end is going to be good? It is like arguing that you take the front end of a car off and expect it to run.
The Federal Court has rendered a decision-

speechtext: Which end are you referring to?
Which end are you speaking from?

speechtext: Order. Perhaps the hon. member could put his question.

Mr. Speaker, my question is again directed to the minister. She has a responsibility to take this Federal Court decision in the serious context that it was given. Does she not believe that, together with the other condemnations of her system, this judicial ruling is serious enough for her not to continue with business as usual, but to suspend those systems currently in place, to try to develop a system that is fair and to try to give justice to individuals who have been waiting in this backlog for some four to five years? I would also remind him that one of the reasons that there are so many people waiting is that the members of his party in the other place, not for the last time I may add, held up something so that thousands and thousands of people were added to this backlog.

This is not the first time that this government has bungled on this matter, either before the Senate's work or after the Senate's work.
March 7, 1990

I would ask the minister whether, in view of the hardship visited on people for some years now, including the members of her own immigration staff, and in view of this added delay for which she is responsible through that guideline, she will direct her staff to prepare a speedy system for landing all persons in that backlog according to basic criteria of health and security.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member is really interested in fairness, he will know that the case-by-case review we are conducting on the backlog is consistent with the legislation now in place which is functioning for people who are arriving in Canada today. A case-by-case method is the most fair way of dealing with people in the backlog.
It is our view, in keeping with natural principles of the rule of law and case-by-case, that this is the way to conduct the backlog despite the difficulties. Our job is to try to overcome any of those difficulties in the process as they arise.

Mr. Speaker, the minister knows that her $100 million two year program has now become more like a $600 million six year program. Therefore, the fairness that she undertook is simply not available to these people who must wait and to the whole immigration department which is being disrupted by this program and the drain on its staff.
Therefore, will the minister do what I requested before. Will she at least undertake to use the broad guidelines for de facto, long-term residents of Canada which had been in place and operating for years until she interrupted them with her narrow guidelines? Will she direct her staff to begin today to use those broad and lawful guidelines for all persons in the backlog, including the several thousands who were wrongfully rejected?

Oh, oh.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MEETING WITH AFRICAN NATIONAL CONGRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a week ago today, I had the distinct privilege, on behalf of Canada, to meet with Mr. Nelson Mandela on his first voyage outside South Africa since he was confined to prison 27 years ago. I want to report to Parliament on our conversations, and also on my brief visit to Namibia, in whose struggle for independence Canada has played such a vital role.
Lusaka, Zambia is the headquarters of the African National Congress in exile. Mr. Mandela came to consult with his national executive, some of whom he had never met. He wanted also to meet those countries and institutions which have played a leading role in the struggle against apartheid. The Prime Minister, whom I represented, was one of the first invited to Lusaka, which is a sign of the respect that Canada has won among the
March 7, 1990

people on the front lines of the fight against apartheid. That is a tribute to the resolve of people throughout this House and across the country. But it also creates a responsibility for Canadians to continue our leadership in new circumstances which, while more promising than the decades of impasse on apartheid, are also more challenging and complex.

The House knows the changes which have swept South Africa in recent months:
-the historic Harare Declaration of the African National Congress which accepted the desirability of peaceful, negotiated change in South Africa;
-the election as President of South Africa of F.W. De Klerk, a man who seems committed to initiating real change;
-the unbanning of the African National Congress;
-and the triumphant release of Nelson Mandela from prison on February 11.
The stage is now set for historic progress towards a truly democratic and non-racial South Africa. But we have only just begun. The state of emergency is still in force. Political prisoners remain detained. The pillars of apartheid remain. As Kenneth Kaunda said in Lusaka, Mr. Mandela is now free, but he is free only to live in an apartheid system.

I think it important that Canadians understand the spirit in which Nelson Mandela approaches this phase of events in South Africa. He referred to his meetings with President de Klerk, and the Ministers of Justice and Constitutional Affairs of South Africa, and said he is convinced that they are true reformers who seek a new social contract in South Africa. But, he noted, these are but three men who face the same party structure responsible for the development and the maintenance of the repressive regime of apartheid. They deserve to be encouraged, but neither he nor the world could ignore the history of the national party or the forces of retrenchment which lie in waiting. Mr. Mandela believes that pressures must be maintained until real change occurs. Expressions of intent are not enough to warrant relaxation of pressure.
Routine Proceedings
Mr. Mandela was unambiguous on this issue: the greatest assistance which could be offered by the outside world to the African National Congress is to maintain sanctions. Indeed, he spoke of intensifying sanctions, and I have asked him to indicate where and how he thinks this should occur.
Commonwealth heads of government, in Kuala Lam-pur last year, agreed that Commonwealth pressure would remain unyielding until there was "evidence of clear and irreversible change." The Commonwealth Committee of Foreign Ministers, which I chair, will meet in Nigeria, in May, to assess the evidence of change. The African National Congress has agreed to work with us in that process.
The headquarters of the African National Congress will return to South Africa and the organization, unbanned, will lead the effort to secure a non-racial democracy in South Africa. Thousands of ANC members and followers will have to be relocated inside South Africa. Offices will have to be established. A new infrastructure must be built. The ANC, at the same time it is negotiating, will also have to focus on equipping the black leadership in South Africa for the responsibilities of economic management and political governance.
The ANC asked me for Canada's direct assistance in meeting the costs of its reintegration into political life inside South Africa. I noted the firm policy of successive governments of Canada not to support political parties in other countries. We will, naturally, continue to support specific humanitarian, education and other programs which meet the needs of the ANC. A delegation from the African National Congress will come to Ottawa within a month to discuss specific areas of co-operation.
I also made the point that there are thousands of private citizens in Canada who would want to support the return home of the African National Congress. This resource should be tapped, and I have initiated discussions with representatives of the three parties in Parliament to identify individuals and strategies which can be offered to the ANC to help them secure substantial private Canadian support.
A great challenge facing the ANC is to level the playing field as it approaches negotiations with the government. The South African government will be able to draw on all the wealth, expertise and resources which apartheid has put at its disposal. The ANC is dispos-

March 7, 1990
Routine Proceedings
sessed and disadvantaged in this regard. Successful negotiations will require a greater equality of resources and expertise. That is an area where Canada can help.
Finally, the ultimate success of a non-racial South Africa will depend on the capacity of both blacks and whites to exercise both political and economic power. Economic exploitation lies at the heart of apartheid and, by and large, black South Africans have been shut out of the experience of running industries and businesses. Therefore, I told Mr. Mandela that we will look urgently at additional programs to provide potential black leaders of industry with practical experience in running large corporations in both the private sector and the public sector.
In their telephone conversation of February 13, the Prime Minister invited Mr. Mandela to visit Canada. He has suggested that it might be appropriate for Nelson Mandela to address this free Parliament. Mr. Mandela looks forward to coming to Canada to express directly his appreciation of the support of Canadians.
The impression I took away from two days of meetings is of a man who is strong, serene, wise and generous. He is a person of principle, but also of practicality and flexibility. To emerge from prison after so long a punishment and to retain an understanding of the concerns of his jailers is extraordinary. Mr. Mandela disproves the notion that history is made only by impersonal forces. The course of South African history will be determined in large measure by this man and by his counterpart in Pretoria.
Canada will maintain sanctions until there is clear evidence of irreversible change in the apartheid system. But we intend also to encourage President de Klerk in his courageous and moderate course. Foreign Minister Pik Botha has written to me suggesting that Canadian experience might be particularly helpful in developing negotiated solutions for South Africa. I have responded by proposing that Mr. Ted Lee, the head of our legal branch, and Canada's former Ambassador to South Africa, visit the region to assess areas where Canadian expertise might be of use. I made it clear to Mr. Botha that any expertise we might offer must be available to all
parties in the negotiations. Mr. Lee will be in South Africa in early April to consult with the government, the ANC and other relevant parties.
The nature of the South African challenge has changed. The opponents of apartheid outside South Africa must be as sensitive and generous in encouraging the process of change as Nelson Mandela has been in leading it. Canadian non-governmental organizations have brought great honour to Canada in their fight against apartheid. I will be meeting with them within the next two weeks to discuss how Canadians together can best pursue this fresh prospect of finally ending apartheid.
After my meetings in Lusaka, I paid a brief visit to Namibia, which will celebrate its hard-won independence on March 21. Canada will be represented at the independent celebrations by my colleague, the Minister of External Relations and International Development and by a small all-party delegation from Parliament. For years, Namibian independence was a hostage to apartheid; now Namibia is leading the way for its neighbour South Africa. It is a remarkable example of a successful transition to a non-racial democracy, of the holding of successful free elections, of the drafting of a constitution without peer in Africa. The Namibian success points to what is possible when reason overcomes emotion and compromise replaces prejudice.
During my conversations with President-elect San Nujoma and his ministers-designate, I expressed both Canada's congratulations and our intent to continue to contribute to the development of a stable and prosperous Namibia.
When I was called to the platform to welcome Nelson Mandela to Zambia, President Kaunda said that Canada, though far away, had earned the right to be considered a "front line state" in the fight against apartheid. Because we are a western democracy, a diverse society, a successful economy, our role may be even more important in this sensitive new phase of the campaign to establish a non-racial democracy in South Africa.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to extend to the minister our appreciation for his willingness to address the House,
March 7, 1990

whenever possible, on matters pertaining to foreign affairs.
We Liberals welcome the minister's efforts to meet with Nelson Mandela at an early time. It is important that Canada maintain a high profile in the international effort to persuade South Africa to abandon apartheid. The Liberal Party is currently of the view that recent developments, while encouraging, cannot mask the reality that apartheid is still practised as a rule of law in South Africa. Therefore, we share Mr. Mandela's view that now is not the time to relax sanctions against the South African government.
We on this side of the House feel no need to soften our opposition to apartheid and those forces that support that policy now that Nelson Mandela is finally free. I know the minister will agree with our position stated recently by our Leader that "Apartheid cannot be reformed. It must be abolished."
I know the minister would also agree that will only be possible if the South African government moves to lift the state of emergency, release all remaining political prisoners, and repeal all legislation which give the legal framework to institutionalize racism in South Africa, including the Population Registration Act, the Group Areas Act, the Land Act, as well as the entrenchment in law of segregated health care and education and the homeland system.
As Canadians, we cannot be satisfied with the stated good intentions of the de Klerk government, including its support for negotiations with the African National Congress. As recently outlined by the South African President on February 2, we know very well from experience that promises to hold negotiations are no substitute for actually sitting down at the table. Negotiations once begun can always be broken off.
I suggest, therefore, that the acid test of the South African government's commitment to abandoning apartheid-the only test that Canadians should abide by in considering any change to our sanctions policy-would be their actions during these negotiations, including their position on repealing apartheid legislation.
I would hope that the minister made these points, or will make these points, clear to the South African
Routine Proceedings
government so that there can be no misunderstanding as to where Canada stands now on this issue.
As to the minister's suggestions to Mr. Mandela that he consider renouncing the arms struggle as an instrument of the African National Congress in its battle to make South Africa a truly democratic and non-racial society, Liberals support that view. I will remind the minister that our leader, Mr. TUrner, made that point very clear in his meeting with the ANC president, Oliver Tambo when Mr. Tambo was in Ottawa three years ago.
The Liberal Party would like to encourage the minister to follow through with his offer of continued assistance to ANC sponsored projects in South Africa and other programs designated to help the victims of apartheid. We would hope that these efforts are not compromised because of the government's continued cuts in foreign aid.
As far as the African National Congress as a political party, I want to assure the minister that we will certainly co-operate with his effort. We are willing to participate in whatever actions or non-partisan committees that could be created for this effort. Therefore, I want to inform this House that Senator, the Hon. Alasdair Graham, has been designated by our party to participate on our behalf in any discussions leading to the creation of a private, non-partisan Canadian group of supporters for the ANC.
I do hope that these private efforts will not be a substitute for whatever actions or direct help that could come from the Canadian government in other activities that are not of a political nature.
Finally, I would like to make a short comment on the minister's visit to Namibia after his meeting with Mr. Mandela. Like all Canadians, we share a sense of joy in the birth of that nation to be officially celebrated on March 31. We will move immediately to extend a hand of welcome to Namibia, to the councils of the Commonwealth and the United Nations. I would also hope that the Government of Canada would consider Namibia a priority for continued economic assistance.
I am concerned, however, about the continued uncertainty surrounding the status of Walvis Bay, the only major seaport in Namibia. I would have expected that the minister discussed this matter while in Windhoek, making clear Canada's view that South Africa must return control of that port to the Namibian people.

Routine Proceedings
As I did not hear the minister speak to this issue in his statement today, I would like to ask him if he could inform the House as soon as possible what is happening with that situation, and what Canada could do to help facilitate Namibian efforts to gain control over this port, so clearly vital to their economic growth.
In closing, let me thank the minister on behalf of many Canadians, not only members of Parliament but Canadians throughout the country who appreciate his work and his effort as Chairman of the Commonwealth Committee of Foreign Ministers. What he is doing is very important and appreciated. But I want to remind him that the work is far from being finished. There is still a lot to be done. It will take skill, determination and certainly not to conclude too quickly that the work is over. I wish him well in his efforts.

subsubtopic: MEETING WITH AFRICAN NATIONAL CONGRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by thanking the minister for making a statement in the House, as is his habit, and a welcome habit at that, it gives everyone an opportunity to comment from time to time and to hear each other out on a variety of issues.
All of us felt a tremendous sense of relief and celebration on February 11 when Nelson Mandela was finally released after 27 years in prison. Events surrounding that day and other events in South Africa remind me of the biblical passage which speaks of setting the captives free and giving sight to the blind; the captive in this case being Mr. Mandela and the blind being the white community in South Africa. We hope that the vision of the white community in South Africa will continue to improve and grow towards the day when we have a non-racial democracy in South Africa. We hope that captives will continue to be freed and that all political prisoners in South Africa very soon will be released.
I was mindful, while listening to the minister, of the opportunity I had along with other Canadian parliamentarians, including the hon. member for Waterloo who is here in the House today, to meet with members of the ANC in Lusaka during a visit to that city on our way home from Namibia in September last year. Many of the people we met with on that day for lunch had not been able to be physically present in their homeland of South Africa, for periods of almost as long as three decades. I
am very happy to think that many of them may be able to return to South Africa and that Canada, either through the government or through the arrangement that the minister spoke of through fund raising in Canada, might be able to facilitate that return, both of those individuals and the ANC now that it is longer banned in South Africa.
The minister made the point that what has happened so far is only a start and certainly this is indisputable. The structures of apartheid remain. As I mentioned before, there are many prisoners still to be released who are still detained, and the state of emergency remains. All these things remain to be done.
Nevertheless, I do not think anyone would contest that this is a period of great hope and expectation. That period of hope and expectation is largely related to the remarkable person and personality of Mr. Mandela. I think in many respects he was an unknown as long as he was in prison, but having been released, has now emerged as a person with a strength of character which in a variety of ways may just be able to bridge, along with the obvious abilities of Mr. de Klerk, what sometimes seems like an unbridgeable gap in South Africa. We hope that these two people and others will be able to successfully contend with the forces in both their camps and be able to come to a successful negotiation in the near future.
With respect to sanctions, it is not just a question of maintaining sanctions. It is also a question of more effectively enforcing those sanctions which are already in place. This is something that I know that the committee which the minister heads has addressed itself to and which it should address itself to even more thoroughly in the upcoming meeting.
It may also be a question of intensifying sanctions, something the minister acknowledges in his statement, if indeed that is what Mr. Mandela and others come to request. If that request is made, then I would suggest that the government would have to consider complying with that request. That remains to be seen.
These will be difficult times in the homelands. I was just looking at the news before I came into the House and saw that violence has broken out in another homeland, in addition to the violence that already broke out in Ciskei.
March 7, 1990

There are going to be a great many negative images as well as positive images on the television screen and in the news about South Africa. We should be clear that none of what we see should dilute our resolve to see the democratization process through, and that this is a time for a great deal of patience and understanding.
The minister spoke of the reception which Canada received in Lusaka and the honour which has been brought to Canada. I would like to emphasize that the honour which has been brought to Canada and the honour in which Canada is held by the leadership in Africa with respect to the anti-apartheid struggle is due in large part to a variety of Canadians all across the country; and to non-governmental organizations, churches and coalitions that have been struggling along for years trying to bring attention to this problem.
In many respects, without wanting to be too partisan about it, they have been pushing governments to take the lead and to do more. Certainly, their work has paid off in what the Canadian government has done so far and what we hope the Canadian government will do in the years to come. It is because ordinary Canadians have been seized with this issue and have refused to drop it that governments over the years have been forced to pay attention to this issue. It is no less so in the United States of America where black Americans have made this an issue which has forced successive American governments to pay attention. In this respect I was glad to see that there was a relative absence of self-congratulation in the statement. The credit that has come to Canada in terms of the anti-apartheid struggle is a credit that belongs to a great many Canadians and belongs more to the people of Canada than to any particular government.
I was also interested to see the theory of history embedded in the minister's statement when he said that Mr. Mandela had persuaded him that history was not the result of impersonal forces, and that sometimes people can make a difference. I think that is true.
Unfortunately, I feel that way about our country at this point, only on the opposite side of the fence. I feel that way about the Prime Minister. I think that had we a different person in charge of the country, the country

might have a better chance of surviving. But persons do make a difference. In this case it is a negative one.
I would like to say a word about support for the ANC. I am aware of the arrangements being sought by the minister with the three political parties in Canada. I presume that will proceed to some kind of conclusion. But the minister made an interesting point when he said that successive Canadian governments have refused to support political parties in other countries. I think that is a worthy tradition. The government should have used that principled position as a basis on which to criticize the action of the United States in Nicaragua when it chose to fund a political party outside the United States of America, in this case the opposition which recently won the election. The minister will know that I asked him to do that in committee. I still have not heard any words of criticism in that regard. If this is a principle worthy of upholding in Canada and by the Canadian government, perhaps it is something we should suggest to our neighbours.
With respect to Namibia I would like to begin by congratulating the great many Canadians who have been involved in that struggle and, of late, those many RCMP officers who I am sure had an incredibly different experience in Namibia, some of whom recently received an award as a result of their work there. Perhaps some day members of Parliament might have an opportunity to sit down with some of the officers who served there. I think it would be a good idea to get a feeling for the experience they had.
Namibia is one of the great successes of the United Nations, of the international community and of reconciliation. I remember coming out of Namibia in September feeling myself that this thing was going to work, and that the only thing that might cause it not to work was people continuing to mistrust each other. There were certain people who could not believe that South Africa might actually allow this thing to happen. There were other people who could not believe that SWAPO would not think up some devious, violent scheme to intimidate voters in particular areas of the country.
I think those of us who came out of Namibia at that time had the feeling that people had come to the point where they were willing to trust, willing to forgive in many respects, and willing to take a chance on the future. That worked. I hope that is the kind of spirit

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I might indicate that my intention is to have a 10-minute speech and a 5-minute question and answer period and share my time with one of my colleagues.
I am pleased today to take part in the debate approving in general the budgetary policy of the government. This is the sixth budget brought in by the Minister of Finance, and he has continued his record of fiscal responsibility to deal with the legacy of debt left by the previous administration, while at the same time creating the climate for non-inflationary economic growth.
As a result of policies aimed squarely at spending restraint, the government has reduced the deficit from its peak of $38.3 billion in 1984 to $30.5 billion in the last fiscal year. That is a decline of almost $8 billion, and this
March 7, 1990

decline is to continue. Just as important, direct borrowings of the Government of Canada in capital markets are also down about $8 billion since 1984.
In the April 1989 budget the government set out a five-year plan to cut the deficit in half by 1993-1994, to eliminate government borrowings in capital markets after that year, and to begin to pay back government securities, Government of Canada bonds, and other debt instruments securing the debt.
This budget confirms the fact that we are still on a course to meet the goals set out in the last budget. First, it will ensure that the deficit continues on a downward track. Second, it will help to create the conditions needed to ease inflationary pressures. This will lessen the burden on monetary policy and increase the scope for interest rates to come down. Lower interest rates will contribute to further reductions in the deficit, and this will set the stage for the economy to make the transition to strong, sustained growth.
There are three basic points I wish to speak to with regard to the budget. They are interest rates, government spending, and the impact this budget will have on my home province of Ontario. As I mentioned previously, and contrary to what those across the House would say, the high level of interest rates is only a symptom of the over-all problem we face in Canada. The real problem is the underlying inflation which drives up interest rates. There is no magic wand with which to lower interest rates. This would only serve to fuel inflation, thus compounding the problem. If we do not deal with these inflationary problems at this point in time, we could see a return to the economic conditions which persisted in the early 1980s. This includes the recession we know so well that was created. The painful lesson of despair, sinking confidence at home and abroad, and the personal hardships endured by all too many Canadians during that period will not be repeated.
There are may people in my region concerned with the high interest rates. The automobile manufacturers see the high interest rates and the resulting high value of the Canadian dollar as a very real impediment to their ability to compete in the car market. People who work in the construction industry see residential housing and all of their projects affected by high interest rates. Some would
The Budget
even say that the high value of the dollar concerns those merchants who see individuals going to the United States seeking better bargains. These people would like to see interest rates reduced immediately, but they do not want to see the return of the spectre of inflation and high interest rates approaching 20 per cent, haunting them again as it did in the early 1980s. They want to see the cause of high interest rates removed in order that rates will come down and stay down and that their future security will not be threatened. Non-inflationary growth is the goal that this budget helps to accomplish.
The government has set in place a number of policies in order to expand the potential of the economy for non-inflationary growth. This budget with its emphasis on expenditure control, as well the policies of privatization and deregulation, the free trade agreement, the retraining programs under the Canadian Jobs Strategy, and the replacement of the manufacturers' sales tax with the goods and services tax will result in the potential growth of the economy expanding to 3.25 per cent to 3.5 per cent from the present 2.75 per cent which existed in 1984. Without these changes there was even a danger that the potential for non-inflationary growth in the economy would contract.
Intertwined in this entire matter is the question of expenditure reduction in order to deal with the annual deficit and ultimately the national debt. The national debt is approaching $350 billion and interest on that debt for the current year will be approximately $41.2 billion. Over the last five years the government has managed to turn the deficit in program spending to a surplus of approximately $13 billion. The deficit this year will be $28.5 billion. The budget sets us on a course to continue reduction in this annual deficit in order that we can provide more flexibility to the government to protect programs that Canadians desire.
Presently we spend approximately 35 cents of every tax dollar taken in on interest on the national debt. It is generally acknowledged that approximately 80 per cent of the debt is held here in Canada by our own citizens. However, we still have to this debt to those individuals who hold Canada bonds, treasury bills and other Government of Canada securities. This results in an income

March 7, 1990
The Budget
redistribution program from the taxpayers to those individuals who can afford to buy the Government of Canada securities. This is obviously a type of income redistribution that no one in the country wants. If this process were allowed to continue we would see the government merely taking tax dollars from its citizens and repaying it to individuals who can afford the securities. We would not be able to fund the programs which Canadians want and we would not be able to provide any new programs such as those for the environment, child care, or any other area. The only way continue to attack this problem is through expenditure reduction. The budget tabled by the finance minister is aimed at achieving these goals. It reflects what is necessary in Canada today, living within our means. We cannot continue to spend money we do not have.
These expenditure reductions are being shared by all individuals in Canada. This causes difficulties for people everywhere. The easy course would be simply to continue spending and as a result increase the annual deficit and the national debt and put the day of reckoning on the backs of our children. I do not want to leave that legacy to my children. It is difficult, but I was not elected to be representative of convenience, supporting only those policies that are currently popular and easy. We have to look to the future and ensure that it is a bright one, not clouded by debt inherited by these children from their parents, with the added responsibility of supporting their parents as well. It is incumbent upon the government to take a leadership role and follow a course of action that is responsible both to the people we represent and to future Canadians.
The expenditure control plan outlined in the budget is designed to spare those individuals who personally cannot afford to see transfers reduced. Examples are old age pensions, spouses' allowance pensions and the unemployment insurance program which are exempt. Also exempted are the equalization program and Canada Assistance Program transfers to those provinces receiving equalization. There has also been a freeze in EPF funding. The provinces of Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta are being asked to shoulder a larger proportion of the expenditure reductions at the present time because of their more prosperous positions. Ontario must bear its share of the load because it stands to benefit greatly from a healthier national economy.
Ontario has a great responsibility within Confederation. The debt is a national problem and the country is counting on Ontario to help with its share of this burden.
Since the government took office it has been totally committed to being responsible with spending from the public purse. In that light, it is quite frustrating to see Ontario increase its spending in the last five years by close to 10 per cent per year and increase its public service by over 7,000 individuals, while the federal government has held its own spending to about 3.6 per cent per year over the same period and reduced its Public Service by 12,000 person-years to levels equal to those of the 1970s.
As I mentioned previously, the federal government is paying 35 cents of every revenue dollar just to cover the debt charges.
Critics have said that the freezing of the EPF funding will have a negative impact on the areas of health care and post-secondary education. It is interesting to note, however, there have been no conditions attached to this funding since 1977. The province is free to allocate the money in any manner it wishes. It cannot be said that it goes directly to health care or to post-secondary education when one realizes that the spending of the Government of Ontario increased at the rate of 10 per cent per year. I am sure that they will not have to increase their taxes or increase their deposition, but they can follow the lead of the federal government and cut their expenditures and reallocate their priorities in order that health care and post-secondary education receive the commitment that it should.
The other important fact for Ontario residents is that no new taxes have been proposed in this budget. My constituents have been quite clear in their expectations that expenditure reductions be undertaken and that taxes are not to be increased. The Minister of Finance has definitely listened to the people.
The overriding concern in the country today is the deficit and the national debt. Some people say that the government is preoccupied with this problem and they want to return to the easier, more comfortable days when the government simply ignored the matter and continued its spending and put off the day of reckoning to another generation. This is the easy way out. We cannot return to those policies without inflicting a great deal of damage on the country. This budget illustrates that this government is prepared to stay the course, to see the reduction of the deficit and the ultimate repay-
March 7, 1990

ment of the debt. This is the only action that will ease the inflationary pressures in the economy in order that interest rates can be reduced to an acceptable level, secure programs which Canadians value and set us on a course for sustained growth. This is the type of economic conditions which all Canadians want to create, and they want to see the leadership and courage necessary to ensure that these goals are attained.
This budget will take us into the next century in a strong position to take advantage of the increasingly competitive climate to which we are proceeding in the world. We do not want our children to look back and ask the question why we did not have the courage to deal with the problem when we knew it existed. Indeed this budget shows the courage to make the tough decisions and to do what Canadians have asked: be a government that looks into the future and implements the policies necessary to secure that future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was most interested in my hon. friend's comments. I do not know how he can some of the things that he did with such a straight face, because I am not sure that Canadians are buying it. I have a number of questions for him. Perhaps he could answer them more specifically.
The member talked about this budget and its assumptions. Every major group in this country has questioned the very assumptions that this budget talks about, namely interest rates at 11 per cent. The member knows that current interest rates are 13.5 per cent, that growth rates are unrealistic and that the Minister of Finance has admitted the budget will increase unemployment rates.
Five budgets ago the same Minister of Finance had indicated that if everything had been as he predicted in 1985, the annual deficit would be $15 billion today. Yet we know that he was dead wrong then and is dead wrong now, because we still have a $30 billion deficit.
I wonder if the member could also answer for me why he believes-and he comes from Ontario-Ontario should be penalized. Is it because it is doing such a good job, because it has a surplus in its budget or, as he indicated, because it is spending too much? Which is it? Why penalize the prosperous parts of Canada that in fact
The Budget
make it possible for this country to provide services to the rest of the country?
How could he say to the Canadian people that there are no new taxes in this budget when it specifically mentions the GST to the tune of $1.9 billion and also mentions those other tax measures that were in previous budgets, such as the deindexing of family allowances, personal exemptions, and so on?
I wonder if the member would be good enough to give the straight facts to Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Edwards (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in the budget debate, particularly since I had the opportunity earlier this week, on Sunday evening and Monday, to be a participant in the

March 7, 1990
The Budget
excellent national exercise put on by the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce, a national conference on deficit reduction.
There are three ways in which a country can lose its sovereignty: when it disintegrates internally or from external threat, when it loses its sense of self, or when it loses control of its economic agenda.
This government has put in place long-term strategies to meet each of those challenges. National reconciliation leading to Meech Lake which will bind our country together, honouring and nurturing our cultural institutions, and the agenda for economic renewal announced November 8, 1984 and followed since.
The Meech Lake Accord is at a crossroads of success. Beyond the text and principles of the accord itself the very idea of Canada is being questioned, not just Canada as we know it, because if any significant portion of our country does leave Canada is gone perhaps forever.
We have a fundamental debate going on. What is Canada? Why Canada? What price, Canada? We are at risk of losing our sense of self. We are constantly at that risk. We need a strong national broadcasting system, public, private, educational and community, to show each other to ourselves to foster a Canadian consciousness. We need to encourage in bom Canadians the same awe, pride and humility demonstrated weekly in dozens of citizenship courts throughout the land by those who take the oath of allegiance. All of this is for nought if we lose our way economically.
The budget of February 20,1990 is another logical step toward freeing Canada from the stultifying strait-jacket of debt which threatens to remove our freedom of purpose. If we had not taken stringent action on February 20 there is a scenario which overwhelms one. We would have had interest rates rising to the 13.5 per cent to 16 per cent range over the next two to three years. We would have had a $20 billion long-term overseas placement of debt which in itself would have required a substantial increase in the personal tax and/or extensive cuts in social spending and universality.
There are a great many challenges before us. They have been met in this budget to some extent, but I submit not to the fullest extent. We had measures affecting my own home province of Alberta. We had the
announcement of the termination of the federal government participation in the OSLO project which does not necessarily signal the end of that project.

I listened with interest to my friend from the Niagara Peninsula talking about the Ontario situation and the transfers to Ontario. Alberta is in precisely the same position as Ontario vis-a-vis this budget in terms of the transfer payments. Further to that, our two provinces are affected identically in terms of the elimination of the incentive program for the oil and mining industries. We are all sharing. We are asking the provinces to share in the burden that we have assumed ourselves at the federal level. The economic agenda has comprised the free trade agreement, the privatization initiatives and tax reform.
