speechtext:
Here is the verdict from a journalist of The Edmonton Journal, Mark Lisac, who is not known as a fan of the current Government of Canada. He wrote:
The next time the Chamber of Commerce invites Finance Minister Michael Wilson it should have him pick on someone his own intellectual size, or somewhere close to it.
The article continued:
Wilson did well on a radio phone-in show earlier in the day too. I don't know how the GST idea stands up after his visit to Alberta, but we sure saw a demonstration of political leadership.
With all the budget and all the tax reform there is an underlying concern in the nation. It is summarized in a letter I received in my office just the other day from a constituent who wrote:
I wish to respond to your reply to my wife's McDonald's GST Coupon, which was an eye opener for myself.
March 7, 1990

Subsequent to your explanation I have jumped off the "Band Wagon" of resistance to the GST in view of my enlightenment.
Because I was not aware of all the factors and considerations associated with MST and the GST I naturally resisted change and seemingly unwarranted tax. After discussion with my wife and with an urgent desire to protect our children's future we have decided that we would prefer to see GST applied to restaurant meals at a higher rate rather than having a higher GST rate applied to basic groceries and goods. We do appreciate the need for GST if our commitment to lower the deficit is sincere.
There is the nub of the entire debate. My sense of the mood across the country, particularly in Alberta, is: "Look, we will support this idea of tax reform if you folks are serious about wrestling the deficit to the ground". That was reinforced by the work of the national conference on deficit reduction held on Sunday and Monday of this week.
The summation of the findings of the various committees of that conference was as follows. On the issues of government administration, the advice of Mr. Joe Martin, the rapporteur of that particular committee, was that government should get out of operations and back into governing; that all Canadians should recognize, all of us, the limits of government; that there should be an elimination of duplication among levels of government; that certain privatization initiatives should take place, such as the privatization of airports; that the following services should be contracted out: tax collection, prisons and payrolls; and that consideration should be given to turning Public Works Canada and Supply and Services Canada into Crown corporations in order to put their operations on a more rational basis.
The distinguished economist Dr. Maureen Farrow reported on social programs. She came to the observation that many of the programs which we have in place today were founded in the 1960s and met a 1960s situation. They were programs designed to frustrate regional adjustment to a dynamic economy. She said that incentives must encourage adjustment and universality should be amended and shifted to targeting. She favoured addressing the insufficiencies and the inefficiencies in such programs as health care. As well, she felt that all social programs should be capped as of today in current dollar terms, that governments should then re-allocate the diminishing thought using in-house skill
The Budget
sets, that time and notice should be given to Canadians in pension schemes so that they could make adjustments to real market conditions. No more indexation, said she, and all Canadians should begin to manage their expectations.

No, this was not a Tory caucus meeting. This was a national conference on deficit reduction.
The summation of the conference was given by the distinguished management consultant and financial adviser, Mr. W. D. Grace, who chaired the economic affairs committee. He concluded that the Government of Canada should immediately put a cap on spending at the current $103 billion, that there should be appointed a non-profit broad-based body to publicize the deficit to condition Canadians to the problem that is before us, the threat of the debt, and then evaluate and publicize all items of government spending. I believe that the Auditor General would be of great assistance in this regard.
I summarize the findings of the National Conference on Deficit Reduction held in Edmonton this week to indicate to friends, particularly friends opposite, that it is not a grinch budget that we have before us, but rather that a strong body of Canadians are calling for a further diminishing of the expectations of Canadians and what the Government of Canada does for them and to them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the questions of my friend opposite. In response to his second set of questions, the whole idea of tax reform as we have it before us now is designed to impact favourably on lower and middle-income Canadians. It is a demonstrable fact which no one, including the renowned Liberal finance critic, has been able to rebut. Canadians with an income of less than $30,000 will be better off after tax reform than before.
Insofar as Albertans are concerned, as the Minister of Finance indicated in the debate on Monday night, the manufacturers' sales tax siphoned $685 per Canadian, per Albertan, out of the province of Alberta. The goods and services tax will mean a net increase of $5 for the average Canadian out of Alberta. But in terms of economic growth, and this is what our Liberal friends forget, the tax reform measures moving from the MST to the GST are the greatest net benefit to the province of Alberta, with projected economic growth of just under 3 per cent as opposed to the national average of something under 2 per cent.
My friend refers to polls that were taken following the debate. I was not aware of the one he refers to but I would refer him to the one taken by K 97, another distinguished Edmonton medium, which found that 98 per cent of those who watched the debate found that they did not believe the Liberal finance critic. They did not believe him, let alone saying who won the debate.
Now, if you were to examine the Edmonton Convention Centre floor you would find that even the most distinguished caretaking and custodial staff have not been able to remove the gore of the Liberal finance critic from that floor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased at the opportunity to express my concerns regarding this budget.
Along with my colleagues I am honoured to represent in this House the voice of Canadians whose needs and concerns have been ignored by the government in its plans. When I look over this budget I see negative, regressive policies in almost every area. What really jumps off the page is the way that a supposedly national government is making the most vulnerable groups of Canadians bear the brunt of its mania to cut the deficit. These groups include veterans, women, natives and people who live in geographically and economically isolated regions of Canada.
The Minister of Finance is very fond of telling Canadians that we must all join in the effort to cut the deficit and the public debt. Average Canadians suffered under last year's budget and will continue to suffer under this year's budget as well as under other policies introduced by this government.
My colleagues on this side of the House have done a very thorough job of showing how this budget will hurt Canadians without doing much to help our deficit and debt situation, so I intend for a few minutes to discuss several areas of special concern to me and my constituents.
While all Canadians view the government's policies and plans apprehensively, Atlantic Canadians have even more reason to be suspicious of this government's action. In the weeks leading up to the 1990 budget we remembered how our region was hammered in last year's budget. Having given our pound of flesh last year we dared to hope that the government would make some attempt to help the Atlantic region as it enters an economic crisis of unprecedented proportions. I refer not only to the fisheries crisis, but also to our high unemployment level, to the effects that the base closures and reductions are already having on our economic growth, to the slashing of our rail services, to the changes to the unemployment insurance program and to the fundamental sense of alienation on the part of Atlantic Canadians. We feel this way because we have seen no evidence during the past year that the government cares about this region. The failure of the government to include an Atlantic aid package in this budget plus its continued neglect of regional development only deepens the feeling of anger and of alienation.
	
March 7, 1990

Last year's budget promised continued high levels of regional development spending, but what followed was cut-backs to the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, which the government tried to disguise by stretching ACOA's mandate without allocating more funds. Having seen through this smokescreen one can understand why Atlantic Canadians are suspicious of the government's plans for the continuance of ACOA. The recent budget announced that ACOA grants would be eliminated and that ACOA would only provide loans in the future. This was unacceptable, since entrepreneurs in the region need the government's support in their endeavours more than their counterparts do in central Canada, for obvious reasons. So, the government modified slightly its harsh stance by announcing that changes will be made in ACOA's project funding criteria, which will allow it to provide grants in some cases and which will raise the ceiling for direct contributions to projects. This is a positive move. However, to prove that it has a firm commitment to Atlantic development, the government must stop sending out mixed signals. Regional development policy is fundamentally altered on a regular basis. It seems to follow a patchwork strategy and constant change means that the Atlantic business community is always having to second guess itself. This is hardly a sound regional development strategy.
Atlantic Canadians are receiving very clear signals that the government is abandoning our transportation infrastructure. First, the government killed VIA Rail which is vital to a region which needs affordable, accessible rail travel.
Now it starts to whittle away at Marine Atlantic, the Crown corporation which operates ferry services in Atlantic Canada. Marine Atlantic will lose over $9 million in the next two years, a move which will result in either reduced services or higher fees, neither of which is good for passengers or business in this region. Prince Edward Island's economy in particular will suffer from this decision.
Another step in the government's abandonment of the region's transportation infrastructure is the cut-back in small craft harbours. The program will lose $29 million over the next five years. As well, the budget announces that the government will: "implement alternative management and operational policies for existing harbours". Are we to infer that this means the privatization of small craft harbours or higher user fees for fishermen? This
The Budget
simply cannot be borne. Our communities are already under siege.
"Under siege" is a good way to describe how all Canadians feel about the budget cut-backs in Established Programs Financing which contributes to provincial health care and post-secondary education.
If a budget is a symbol of a government's priorities and values then this measure is a sad comment on the soul of this government. The finance minister's rallying cry that we must all help to fight the deficit takes on a whole new meaning. He means that deficit reduction will be carried on the backs of the young and the sick.
Let me add my voice to the chorus of outrage against this government's appalling lack of compassion and respect for veterans. It cannot be stressed enough that Canadians owe these men and women a debt which can never be fully repaid. They fought or were willing to fight for their country only to see now the government which claims to represent that country turn on them. In our time of need they were there. Where is the government in their time of need? The government plans to charge board and lodging to approximately 1,500 veterans under long term care and it will increase the rates for those already paying. The government carries this outrage one step further by eliminating the heavy housecleaning program that helped veterans live in their own homes. This government intends not only to deprive veterans of affordable long term care but of their dignity and independence as well. Having already fought for Canada, veterans should not be enlisted in the so-called war against the deficit.
All Canadians are questioning why they have been drafted to fight a war that they did not instigate. The Conservative government has had six years of economic growth and increasing revenues, but we have also had six years of Tory mismanagement of Canada's economy and finances. Now, as the country slides into a recession, we are hit with another bad news budget. The Tories will say it could have been worse, and Canadians shudder at the very thought.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has raised many interesting points in his budget discourse. I have a comment and a question for him.

March 7, 1990
The Budget
The debt that the government inherited in 1984, roughly $170 billion, of course has suffered the evils of compound interest over the years, and about 80 per cent of the additional debt that has been added is due to that interest factor. The debt, as we all know, now stands at around $350 billion a year which is appalling by all our standards. To service that debt this year will take interest of roughly $41 billion.
As has been pointed out in this Chamber this afternoon, that money mostly will be paid to Canadians. It will mostly be paid to Canadians who hold Government of Canada bonds and treasury bills. Now, these are not in general poor Canadians. They are generally wealthy Canadians. They are wealthy investors who have had the extra money to invest in treasury bills and bonds.
It seems to me that this is a massive transfer of money from taxpayers to wealthy investors. I do not understand why the opposition members are not hollering about this amazing transfer of wealth from the have-nots to the haves. They keep saying the Tories are doing things for their rich friends. But this is wrong. This is bad social policy to be transferring tax money into the bank accounts of the wealthy.
Would my hon. friend not agree that this practice has to end quickly? If he does not accept the government's way of doing it, what is his alternative?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend for his comments and questions. As we talk about ordinary Canadians and wealthy Canadians, there are many ordinary Canadians who buy Canada Savings Bonds, and pick up money in this way.
My concern about the whole deficit reduction plan in general is, as I have said in many, many speeches in this Chamber, that we have heard this hue and cry every day about deficit reduction. We hear about putting more debt onto the middle and low income people. I still have not got an answer to the question that I have raised so many times, about why, when we went through a period of five years of great economic growth where the government had billions of dollars in surplus funds, we are in this deficit situation today.
Why was it not at least taken care of at that time instead of letting it grow so that that transfer of money to wealthy Canadians continued on through that period?
I know that ordinary men and women out on that street, everybody, is concerned about this debt. We wish that we could wave the magic wand, but I am afraid that is not possible. We all have to suffer this burden and do everything we can to bring it down.
My question over the last number of months has been why greater concern was not paid to this from 1984 to 1989. Suddenly, through no fault of the government in particular, the economy is going into a tailspin. Now, at all costs, we have to do things that we should not be doing at this time in our lives. We should not be raising interest rates. We are into a tight economic situation and at the same time the poor are taxed even further because we have to reduce this deficit. I just cannot understand why it could not have been done earlier when times were better.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate. The hon. member for Winnipeg North.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the annual statement of the Minister of Finance reflects the mind and the heart of the government of the day. In this context, budget '90 reflects to Canadians the lack of candour of this Tory government and the uncaring attitude with which it treats the most vulnerable members of our society.
Where, one may ask, is the evidence? I refer my hon. colleagues to the statement of the hon. Minister of Finance. Referring to the expenditure control plan of the government, he said:
In designing the measures we were sensitive to the financial circumstances of individual Canadians as well as governments. We have exempted major transfers to persons. These include elderly benefits, family allowances, veterans' allowances and unemployment insurance benefits.
The truth has to be fully said. This government has just finished hitting these programs this past year, and it has recently pushed through this House the clawbacks on baby bonuses and old age pensions and the unemployment insurance restrictions, despite great concerns raised by the Liberal opposition. Now this government has the gall to proclaim that it has exempted these benefits from the cuts in this year's incoming budget.
This is the first piece of evidence of the hypocrisy of this budget.
March 7, 1990

"There will be no new taxes in this budget", said the Minister of Finance. Does this government really think that Canadians can be made to believe that the GST which is becoming more properly known as the gouge and squeeze tax is not an inherent part of this proposed budget? All provincial governments have complained about this proposed tax measure. This government has responded by passing to the provinces the burden of greater expenditures to maintain their social programs at current levels. The provincial governments therefore face the unpleasant task of having to increase their own taxes. This is the second set of evidence of this government's hypocrisy.
Parenthetically, this government has in the last six years introduced an average of five different tax increases per year, now a total of 32 tax increases over this period of time.
The third piece of evidence for lack of candour on the part of this government is reflected in the action it took last December when it withdrew its promise to reduce the tax rate for middle income Canadians. On top of this the surtax was increased from 3 per cent to 5 per cent.
There are many more signs of this government's lack of candour. Due to the time constraints allotted to me, I can only discuss one more piece of evidence and it is very relevant to the question asked by my colleague from the government side to my colleague who just spoke before me.
The Tory government has portrayed the impact of our national public debt as though it entails the same burdens and dangers as the debts of private individuals and business companies, of provincial and municipal governments, and of a host of Third World developing countries.
The total national debt is not essentially the same as these other debts. Professor Ruben C. Bellan, an Emeritus Professor of Economics writing for Policy Options, issue of January-February, 1990, reminded us that only one of the categories of obligations comprising the total national debt truly corresponds to the types of debt I have alluded to above.
What are the facts? In 1988 the government paid the Bank of Canada $2,110 billion as interest on bonds it held. The bank, after taking into account its operating expenses for the year, handed over $1,938 billion back to
The Budget
the government. The government did not point out that it got back 92 per cent in revenue of the interest paid by the Bank of Canada.
The government also failed to point out that it collected a lot of revenue from the same Canadian public to whom it paid billions of dollars in interest on the bonds that Canadian taxpayers hold. They are not necessarily wealthy Canadians. A significant number of ordinary Canadians like to save with Canada Savings Bonds.
The Minister of Finance said:
This year alone interest payments will cost us close to $40 billion,
equal to $1,500 for each and every Canadian.
The minister failed to advise us that a significant component of this debt paid was returned to the government as revenues through the Bank of Canada or as taxes collected from Canadian bond holders. He failed to advise us that the government paid interest to non-Canadian residents on only 16 per cent of bonds denominated in Canadian dollars and that the debt owing to non-residents in 1988 which was payable in foreign currencies was only 4 per cent of the total national debt. Failure on the part of this government to fully disclose all essential financial information and analyses is tantamount to misleading the Canadian public, that is, that the total payment on interest are debts paid without corresponding government revenues.
In other words, the government magnified the fear in the belief that we could buy this budget even if it is a budgetary policy sans sensitivity and heart.
This government has used the absolute magnitude of the total national debt as an excuse to sell this heartless budget, invoking that ultimately we would not be able to pursue our social policies and programs.
As Professor Bellan points out, if one looks at the facts they contradict frequently made statements that the consequences of federal budget deficits are completely negative, "that they are responsible for high interest rates and inflation, that the government's borrowing to finance them 'crowds out' private borrowers from the country's capital markets."
The financial and fiscal history of Canada in recent times does not corroborate the assumptions of this government. The series of large deficits that has occurred since 1981 has been accompanied by a reduction in the Canadian rates of interest and inflation rate, and

March 7, 1990
The Budget
by increases in the amount of capital made available to the private sector by the country's financial institutions".
In fact, when the record is further considered, it becomes obvious that large deficits have not severely limited policy options. Professor Bellan has correctly pointed out that "Canada's national debt has increased 70-fold since 1939 and interest payments are now 200 times higher than what they were in that year. Yet, in 1939 the federal government did far less for Canadians than it does today." Indeed, today the government of our country maintains three major programs-unemployment insurance, family allowances, and medicare-that did not exist in 1939 and contributes far more to education and welfare.
Speaking of welfare and other forms of social assistance programs, this government has tried to excuse itself for capping the Canada Assistance Plan ceilings by saying that the cap only affects the three richest provinces.
Well, we know that the Canada Assistance Plan is the funding program for welfare payments and services to the poor and that half of Canada's poor live in those three richest provinces. Therefore, they stand to suffer, as correctly observed by Mr. Leonard Shiffrin of the Winnipeg Free Press, issue of March 1, 1990.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, this government has not been fully candid with Canadians. Not only has the government not been candid, but it has conveniently excused itself to be a government without a heart. It has recently started to chip away at the universality of our social programs and now it has decided to start killing the one program that is completely targeted to the poor. The poor stand to suffer even more when they want to pursue further education and when they get ill.
The freeze on transfer payments in the proposed budget is another blow to Canadians. Three times since 1986 this government has imposed measures that have reined in Established Programs Financing.
If this trend continues, if this Tory government continues its assault on transfer payments to provinces, Ottawa will cease to pay a single penny for medicare in any of the 10 provinces by the end of this decade. When this happens, medicare as we know and cherish it today, will be dead and each province will have its own different health scheme. In each province the system will become
segregated, much like it is in the United States. For the rich there will be a first-class private system. For the poor there will be inefficient, underfunded, overcrowded health care system.
Ten years ago the federal government paid for 51 per cent of the cost of medicare in Ontario. Under this government, it is now 37 per cent. After this new budget, this percentage will continue to decrease.
Transfer payments from Ottawa for my home province of Manitoba are depended upon for 38 per cent of its revenues. While health programs have been increasing between 7 and 9 per cent per year, the transfer payments which cover this vital program have not been increasing at this rate.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to share my views on the government's recent budget. As Associate Minister of National Defence I am going to speak briefly about the budget and Canada's Armed Forces. But first I would like to discuss the budget as it affects Canadian

March 7, 1990
The Budget
women in my role as minister responsible for the status of women.
The government has made a very clear commitment to the women of Canada since it was first elected in 1984. We have honoured this commitment, not just in promises but with real and substantial action.
Since 1984, the number of women in decision-making positions in commissions and agencies of the federal government has increased by 100 per cent. We have set in place a plan for equal pay for work of equal value in the federal Public Service and we have improved the pension benefits for Canadian women.
When we were first elected there were only three women deputy ministers. Today there are 21. Prior to our first election there were fewer than four women ambassadors. Today there are 13. Back then, in the old days, there was only one woman out of the nine on the Supreme Court. Today there are three.
The changes for Canadian women go even further. There has been a decrease of about 757,000 Canadians living in poverty since this government has been in office. This number includes 229,000 women and 259,000 children.
On the job creation side, 61 per cent of the new jobs that have been created have gone to women, a higher ratio than the average entering the workforce. This government improved job training for women to the Canadian Jobs Strategy. We have introduced a $25 million program for immigrant women and improved child tax credits for low-income families.
In 1986, we introduced employment equity legislation, and I sat on that committee. In 1988, we introduced for the first time a $40 million special program initiative to deal with family violence, an issue which causes me a great deal of distress, as I know it does colleagues on all sides of the House.
I am now one of six women in the federal cabinet, when we were first elected there were only two. For the first time in Canadian history there is a woman Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and I congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre.
This government has not neglected the women of Canada. In fact, we plan to do even more and we will do more.
While we must continue to address the needs and rights of Canadian women, we also must address the threat of a large and growing national debt. It must be brought under control if we, as a country, want to continue to grow and prosper. We must continue to reduce the deficit if we are to build a secure future for all Canadians, men and women.
We all know that deficit reduction is not without its pains. All Canadians are contributing to this national effort in order that we secure our economic future. To achieve a lower deficit we need to build a new national partnership that works with an economic agenda and a plan for the future. This budget is part of such a strategy.
A lower deficit means lower inflation, lower interest rates and less of a debt burden. A lower deficit also means we will have more flexibility to make choices about our priorities as Canadians. We will not be bogged down by that debt. For example, we will be able to invest in new programs for the environment, for regional development, for the advancement of women or to lower taxes.
Reducing the deficit is part of a long-term economic plan that is building a stronger and a more competitive economy which is essential for the advancement of women and for their equality.
Canadians have told this government that they want spending cuts. I know my constituents have, as I know they have across the country. We have listened to those Canadians and we have acted on their wishes. In fact, to date, 70 per cent of our deficit reduction has been on the spending side.
As well, as part of the strategy and part of this year's budget, some $1.6 million has been cut from the women's program budget of the Secretary of State. I want to clarify that. Although it is in my colleague's budget I am concerned and involved in that issue.
Some people have said that this will mean the closure of women's centres across the country. I want to make it clear that this government is not closing women's centre. The women's program was not designed to provide funding for social services. That, in effect, is what has happened in certain parts of the country where federal government funding from the Secretary of State has, in effect, been used for the provision of social services, a responsibility, I think we all recognize, of the province.
March 7, 1990

So we have to find new partnerships and assist these centres, where they are providing essential services which are not otherwise available in communities, to continue to work with their local communities in partnership with provincial governments and other sources. In fact, the women's program will work with these centres to help them find other sources of funding.
Under the women's program, under the project funding, there will be increased funds and it is expected that well over 500 projects can be funded, a number of which will obviously be delivered by women's centres. In fact, some of the women's centres in Canada have operated purely on project funding. Other women's centres in Canada have not indeed received any federal funding but have received their support from other levels of government and from the community.
I also want to make it clear that we are not sacrificing local groups at the expense of others. National funding, for example, is not gaining at the expense of local. In fact, four of the national groups have had their core funding discontinued which is in line with the policy to move away from core funding and supporting project funding which requires, of course, accountability for the individual projects.
In addition, the Secretary of State will be redeploying core funding to project funding by reducing four other national groups' budgets by 20 per cent. This redeployment will enable their program to respond to the needs of the most disadvantaged women's groups across the country. When we talk about those we think of the aboriginal women, the new immigrants, the visible minority women and the disabled women, those who really are at a disadvantage and who obviously need the focus of attention the most.
In addition, I am sure that you are aware, Mr. Speaker, that this government continues to support the work of the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, which will be reporting to me, in order that they continue their research, their advice and their advocacy role.
It is worth noting that even after the reductions to the women's program by the Secretary of State, there will be $9.6 million in that program, which is a considerable
The Budget
amount of money and certainly more money than existed when we took office in 1984. It is well over the $8.4 million available at that time. With this money my colleague says that he will be able to support over 500 projects focusing on areas of family violence, economic equality and social justice.
In spite of these cuts, and we know that all areas of government have to participate in this, this government remains committed to the women who need help the most-women who have the double disadvantage of being immigrants, members of visible minorities, women with disabilities and aboriginal women. Those programs in the Department of the Secretary of State remain and some, in fact, have increased funding and will be able to assist, either through women's centres or other programs, work and projects for women in those groups.
We are also committed to ending violence against women, or working towards that. I am not sure we could ever say we can end violence in our society, but we obviously have to work in assisting those women who are victims of violence and work towards eradicating the causes as well.
The reduction in the women's program will not affect our participation in the government-wide initiative to address family violence. These initiatives, led by Health and Welfare Canada, along with five other participating departments, represent a commitment of $40 million over five years by this government. Of this initiative, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation has $22.2 million for capital funding of 500 shelter units.
I can assure the House that this government will continue to support and address the needs of all Canadian women. There are other areas that we will look to in my new areas of responsibility. I will work with my colleagues to identify and address those issues and initiatives that we can move forward with to ensure that women work towards, not only full equality but independence and self-sufficiency in our society. That, I think, is a goal that we all, men and women, share together.
I also have responsibilities with another department and I will move on to that. I would like to spend a few minutes talking about the 1990 budget as it relates to the the Department of National Defence. We now find

March 7, 1990
The Budget
ourselves in a world which is very different from that which we knew a few short years ago or even a few months ago. As a result of the dramatic changes in Europe and the fiscal restraints here at home, we are conducting a review of our current defence policy to ensure that this policy and our program remain sound. The very positive nature of the changes in Europe allow us to take the necessary time to ensure that this review will be thorough and ultimately in the best interests of Canada.
Canada welcomes the prospect of a free and democratic Europe, where the possibility of war, we hope, will be virtually eliminated. This prospect is what we and our allies have been working toward for nearly 50 years. Its development is a tribute in part to the collective efforts of the individual countries of NATO and the members of their armed forces. Canadian servicemen and servicewomen, as well as the civilian employees of DND, should be proud of their contribution to this process.
In our defence policy review, we will examine how we can best fulfil Canada's defence needs in light of our current fiscal realities and in the ever changing international situation.
Needless to say, this review will prove to be a complex process during such a tumultuous time and it is too early to speculate on its outcome. However, I can say that its purpose is to ensure a realistic mandate for the Canadian forces and the resources to do the job.
Obviously we have our work cut out for us. We must reconcile the present fiscal restraints with the still pressing task of reducing the gap between the military commitments and our capabilities in these rapidly changing times.
We are committed to protecting Canada's interests, namely, to contribute to collective security and defence and to play a key role in international peacekeeping. In this role I think not only Canadians but people around the world have recognized the tremendous impact that we have had and the contribution that we make.
As the world changes, so does Canadian society and so must the Canadian forces. Such changes are often difficult but unavoidable.
The Canadian forces are redefining their place in Canadian society and it remains our job to make Canadians understand the crucial role that they will continue to play in the protection of these interests.
I see the maintenance and protection of Canada's interests as a key role for DND. Part of that key role perhaps goes beyond what Canadians traditionally think of when they think of defence.
We need to protect our resources and our territorial integrity.
We must inform Canadians about the role of defence in maintaining our interests.
We must explain to Canadians not just what we are doing now, but what needs to be done and DND's importance in establishing and maintaining sovereignty over the second largest country in the world.
The protection of Canada and Canadians goes beyond boundary patrols. DND must also become more involved in the war on drugs in this country.
The Department of National Defence is committed to doing its part to aid other departments of government in the interdiction of drug traffickers. We are working with the RCMP to track unauthorized or suspicious vessels and aircraft.
In addition, DND has become more involved in protecting our environment.
In 1989, when the forest fires raged through Manitoba, the Canadian forces airlifted close to 6,000 Canadians out of threatened areas within a matter of days. We could say that thousands of lives may indeed have been saved by DND personnel through this initiative.
DND is able to respond to situations like this because we have the equipment and skills to provide security to our country and our citizens.
Now, more than ever, Canadians must come to understand that national defence can and does affect their lives in many positive ways. DND is not and never has been a one-dimensional institution.
Prior to the finance minister's budget there has been a great deal of speculation about the impact of the 1990 federal budget on the Canadian Armed Forces. Some had said that the government had planned to cut our money, affecting upwards of 15,000 members. Others had said that we should reduce or eliminate our resources in Europe. These people were wrong. At this

March 7, 1990

crucial time when our department and our armed forces are being asked to become more flexible and more involved in a wider variety of activities, it would be unwise to allow our numbers to be cut back below a minimum level.
In brief, the defence budget will be reduced by $210 million in this fiscal year and a further $270 million in the following year.
These budget cuts mean that increases in defence spending over the next two years will be limited to 5 per cent, and with inflation currently at the level of more than 5 per cent we will not enjoy real growth but will merely hold the line against inflation in the coming years. Some have called for much deeper cuts. Quite simply, Canada still only spends about 2 per cent of its GNP on defence, compared for example, to the United States which spends about 6 per cent.
There is also a new buzzword in the air; the "peace dividend". Canada has enjoyed this dividend during the past decades, but more dramatically when defence bore the brunt of the government's deficit reduction in April of last year with a $2.74 billion reduction over five years. In fact, when combined with this year's reductions, we have suffered a cut of $3.4 billion over that period.
Canada simply does not have the flexibility which some of our allies enjoy, without seriously damaging the operational effectiveness of the Canadian forces. Yet, we have been able to act in, I think, a responsible fashion to the current fiscal demands.
There will be a reduction of about 1,500 in the size of the regular forces over the next few years. The size of the national Defence quarters will be scaled down and we will reduce our defence liaison staffs in London, England, and in Washington. In addition, reductions in the size of the DND civilian workforce can be expected. No further base closures are expected and capital projects currently under way will likely proceed. But in any future scenario the replacement of equipment for the Canadian forces must remain a high priority.
I would like to remind the House that this government is not prepared to place our sovereignty or security at risk. The current and projected defence budgets represent what this government believes is the essential
The Budget
minimum necessary to safeguard Canada's vital interests.
I would like to say a word as well about the reserves who are such a vital part of this role. We still intend to increase their numbers, improve their equipment and training, assign them to essential and specific tasks and continue to reduce the disparities between the regular and the reserve forces.
We all have a role in helping to resolve the deficit. This government has taken tough but decisive actions. The measures we have taken reflect the seriousness of the situations. We have acted in a responsible fashion.
This budget will build on the achievements of the past five and a half years by working to ensure a more prosperous and secure future for all Canadians. As we achieve more control we will gain greater flexibility and independence of action to act on priorities.
Reducing the deficit will ease the inflationary pressures and create the climate for lower interest rates. This, in turn, will reduce our reliance on foreign investors and strengthen our sovereignty as a nation. The direct results of these actions will be a healthier fiscal position, a healthier economy.
This budget will cut the deficit by half by 1993-1994. It will put the country on a clear path of substantially reducing the burden of debt. Solving our deficit and our inflation problems now will let us build for a secure and rewarding future. It will mean a responsible government with the financial room to manoeuvre, to maintain valued programs and take on new challenges. It will mean a dynamic economy that provides rising living standards and new opportunities.
This budget will mean a confident country that is competitive abroad and in control of its own destiny at home.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the last part of the minister's speech. If I may ask you to depart somewhat from your role at National Defence and make a connection with your responsibility for the Status of Women, when considering the budget cuts, how do you perceive the future role of women within our armed forces, at National Defence? Will they go back to office work? Will your budget cuts affect those who entered the armed forces most recently, including women? How do

March 7, 1990
The Budget
you think women will perceive of your dedication to promoting their status in our armed forces?
As you may have suspected, I am thinking of what happened out West when you congratulated another cabinet minister on his extremely degrading comments about one of our colleagues in the House of Commons. How do you expect Canadian women employed in the armed forces to count on your support, considering budget cuts totalling several million dollars and your comments in Western Canada about the Minister for International Trade?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to respond to what I think is a very important issue and one that I have in just over the past year been very much involved in, that is promoting the role of women within our armed forces.
As the member may be aware, a number of trials had taken place over the previous years to work at integrating women into all roles and occupations in the armed forces. Prior to that time women had been excluded from many trades and occupations because they were said to be non-combative and that women could not do those jobs. That work had been proceeding and there had been actions taken before the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal and the decision of the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal last February was that all trades and occupations should be open to women.
I fully supported that decision and, as you know, the government accepted that decision and said we will proceed with its implementation. I am really pleased to see what is developing within the armed forces. It is not easy because there are areas where women have never been involved before. But I look, for example, at the air force. We have the first two women fighter pilots. I think they are the only ones in the world. We have women in all areas of the air force, even as helicopter pilots. As I go across the country and speak to them, they basically are saying that it is really working well. They are not being discriminated against. They really feel they can aspire now to the highest positions.
Within the navy we face some challenges. There were some real concerns about how it would work with women being on ships and away for perhaps 30 days. There were
concerns for the families back at home as well. We have addressed those. We have tried to concentrate on building up enough women on any ship. Having just one woman on a ship would make it very difficult. We will convert ships slowly and that is working out very well.
Within the army, women are now applying for and being accepted in all the trades and occupations. There are some difficulties in the infantry. We have had a number of women apply who have gone to training and have either dropped out of training or have not been successful. It is an extremely physically demanding occupation. I have been out in the field and it is very strenuous. Many women really do not want that kind of work but some are succeeding. It is going to be important to build up enough of a mass in order that we can really address those issues.
Several months ago I appointed a minister's advisory board on the integration of women in the armed forces. It is made up of very excellent men and women from across the country who will be monitoring the integration of women and advising me on what is happening and if there are problems so that we can make sure that this fully works. We have one of the few armed forces in the world that is actually doing this and many other countries are watching us. So I am very excited by this.
In addition, we have to recognize the special problems and the family responsibilities that many women have. I convened a conference several weeks ago on social issues and the Canadian defence. It is very important for an organization such as ours, the largest government department,-we impact the lives of several hundred thousand people-to really be aware of what the social issues are, the social change that is occurring in society and how we as an organization can be ahead of the game, whether it is family issues, technology issues, or the role of women.
We brought together academics, business people, military people, all sectors. The whole process was very exciting. I see it as the beginning of a process to influence and sensitize our people and other people about what we can do as an organization. I hope that as an organization we are going to be in the very forefront in many of these areas.
March 7, 1990

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I offer my congratulations to the new minister who is responsible for the status of women. It is the first time she has spoken in the House under her new responsibility and I welcome her to that role. I know that we will be working closely together and I shall have a number of questions for her.
The recent budget is a real attack on women. This budget has cut the funding by 100 per cent to almost 80 women's centres across Canada. These women's centres are often the first place a women turns to, a woman who has been battered in her home, a woman who has been sexually assaulted on the street, a woman who has been sexually assaulted in her home. Often the first place they go to is a women's centre. They go to these women's centres because there are dedicated volunteers who have worked in the community, who have correlated information on support services, information on transition homes, and information on counselling services. This is where most often an abused woman will turn to find out what resources are available to her in her community. It is a big step when that woman makes that break through into a woman's centre. Now many of these centres are going to close because of the draconian measures of this government in its budget.
One out of every two women who turns up at a transition home today is turned away because of lack of space. The minister spoke about Project Haven and spoke about the commitment of this government to battered and abused women. But we know that already one out of every two women has the door shut to them when they turn up there, sometimes with their children, looking for sanctuary.
At the same time, this government has increased the budget by $33 million to CSIS. It has increased the budget by $114 million relating to the minister's other responsibility to the Canadian Armed Forces in Europe, at a time when the Berlin Wall is crumbling, at a time when eastern European countries are looking to a more democratic way of life.
I would like to ask the minister how she can justify her position as minister responsible for the status of women in the light of what this government is doing to women? This government is trying to muzzle women. This government has its foot on their throats, and wants to shut women up. How does the minister justifies her role in
The Budget
that government and in that cabinet that is silencing the voices of women?
