subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. minister has only two minutes to answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for her good wishes. I know we will have differences of opinion but I think there are many of these issues we are dealing with that are not really partisan issues. I hope men and women in all parts of this Chamber do care about them and that we can work together. I know particularly on the concerns of women we do share that real concern.
First, I would like to say to the hon. member, because perhaps there is misunderstanding in some areas, that the budgets of the transition houses are not affected by the recent changes in the budget. What is affected is the core funding to the women's centre, which was designed under that program for education and advocacy work. I recognize what happened over the years is that some of them obviously get involved in providing service.
Perhaps this is a good time to make the recognition that the Secretary of State does not have the money to do that. That is not his mandate. His mandate was advocacy, and I think that advocacy has worked very well.
The mandate for looking after and providing services, whether it is counselling or support services for women is the responsibility of a broader group of other levels of government and other programs. We should be addressing those, not just through the Secretary of State's budget, because it does not have those kinds of resources. That, indeed, if I can say to the hon. member, is where we are going to be working with our colleagues at the provincial level, and with colleagues from other departments.
As I mentioned earlier, the family violence fund is there. We will be looking at resources through that. We are looking through other resources in the Secretary of State's department to assist aboriginal and visible minority women.
Could I also say to the hon. member that it has been said there are 77 women centres affected by these reductions. I think approximately 44 of those are in Quebec where the amount of money that is provided by the federal Secretary of State is a very nominal amount of money. It varies $6,000 to $8,000. It does not mean

March 7, 1990
The Budget
that they will close because most of their resources come from other sources.
In British Columbia and Newfoundland, where the primary resources have come from the federal government and the provinces have not been participating to date, we obviously have to look for new partnerships to ensure the provision of services to women, whether it is through women's centres or whether it is through other agencies and communities. This provides us an opportunity to look at these issues. I have been concerned that quite often it has only been poor women who have been looking at these issues. We need to get a lot more women involved and they are going to get my help. I can tell you the women are going to get my commitment to help with these problems and I ask for your support.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I regret the hon. minister's time has expired. Resuming debate with the hon. member for Comox-Albemi.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as it works out, I am very pleased to follow the Associate Minister of Defence in this debate on the budget.
When you look through the concerns that are facing Canada today, I think if you polled Canadians, you would find that 100 per cent of the people in Canada are concerned about the budget. They are concerned about the deficit that this country is facing and what the implications of that deficit are, both for ourselves operating in the present and for our children in the future. What is going to be the future for them if they have to bear the tremendous weight of this deficit that has been built up over a series of governments right through the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s.
In facing the issue of the deficit, we realize on this side of the House, as do members on the government side, that there are basically three alternatives that the minister can take in order to deal with the deficit. He can raise taxes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which he has done 31 times.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Tories definitely know how to raise taxes. My colleague says they have raised taxes 31 times.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: To pay their debt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was always under the impression that when you took over a house and took
over the mortgage, it is now your debt, and you are the one with the responsibility for paying the debt. You assumed the mortgage. You have the responsibility, you have the power, and you are supposed to be developing the programs. It is too late to blame the Liberals. We all know that they were at fault in the previous government. You guys are at fault now and you have the responsibility for dealing with the issue now.
You have raised taxes. Thirty-one times since 1984 this Tory government has raised taxes. I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, from the point of view of the people on this side of the House, there are no further opportunities to raise taxes on the poor and the middle income people in this country.
I am not saying that there is no opportunity to raise taxes, because there are those who, over the last five or six years, as a result of the Tory preference for raising taxes on the poor and middle income people, have escaped taxes altogether.
The wealthiest people in this country, the highest income earners in this country, have actually received a $1,000 dividend on their taxes from this Tory government since 1984. Why is it that the rich get paid and the poor pay more under a Tory government. It is because it is a Tory government.
The other group that got away with paying taxes over the last several years from 1984 until 1990 is those 80,000 to 90,000 profitable corporations, some of the ones that were mentioned by my colleague from Nickel Belt this morning as the top award-winning corporate welfare bums. In spite of the fact that they make profits, in spite of the fact that they do very well, thank you very much, as a result of the tax relief that they are granted, they end up paying no tax at all. As a result, the tax burden in this country is not distributed fairly and a large section of the income earning population of Canada, which has the ability to pay sufficient taxes to help pay down that deficit, is not paying their share. That is why we have such a serious deficit problem in this country.
The other thing that could be done in order to trim the deficit is to cut expenditures. The minister who just spoke is an example of an area of the Canadian government where we can cut expenditures. We all have to take a little bit of the pain when we are talking about

expenditure cuts. In this budget, not everybody is sharing the pain equally.
We had a legitimate right to believe that there was going to be a peace dividend as a result of the reductions in tensions in eastern Europe. Even in the United States and in other of our NATO allies, people are looking at the opportunity for this peace dividend to re-orient their economy, and reduce the heavy expenditures. After all, the expenditure to maintain the defence component of NATO is $957 billion annually. A small percentage of that expenditure would wipe out poverty in Canada this year. A small percentage of that expenditure would wipe out some of the most serious diseases plaguing people on this globe that result in thousands of children dying every single day of starvation and diseases like dysentery which is caused by poor food and water supplies, or the lack of food and water supplies.
With $957 billion our defence system could take a very small percentage of that cut, reallocate it towards other programs, towards helping our children, towards eliminating poverty, towards providing the services that my colleague for New Westminster-Coquitlam was talking about. We could have done a great service to the people of Canada had we taken advantage of that defence dividend in this year, without undermining the effectiveness of our armed forces in doing the things that our armed forces should be doing, and that is protecting Canadian sovereignty, cleaning up the problems of the environment that have been created in Canada, and using our forces deployed internationally at the behest of the United Nations for preserving peace throughout the world and further creating, as a result of that investment in defence forces, an additional peace dividend that we could reap again at home to re-invest in social programs.
One of the ways to deal with this deficit is raise taxes on those who have not been bearing the burden all along. The second way to deal with the deficit is to take advantage of that peace dividend and cut some of the programs that we no longer need as a result of the changes world-wide. The third way to deal with this deficit, and this was an option available to the Minister of Finance, was a gradual reduction in the interest rates that are established in this country. Everybody in this Chamber recognizes that interest rates are far too high. They are stifling our economy. They are making it impossible for people of modest means to buy housing.
The Budget
As a result, it is a serious problem in economic development at home. We need a reduction in interest rates.
In the weeks leading up to the announcement in the budget, I think that a scam was perpetrated on this country by the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and by the Conservative Government of Canada. I will tell you what the scam was. I think it was based on a number of planted stories and a number of actions by government which led Canadians to believe that the burden of deficit cutting was going to be shared equally among all sectors of the Canadian economy and among all sectors of Canadian society. That is precisely what has not happened in this budget.
Let me tell you what the scam amounted to, Mr. Speaker. First, there were the planted stories. You will recall the series in The Globe and Mail and in other newspapers, the interviews with military officers at the Canadian Forces Base at Lahr, interviews with students at the military and officer colleges, interviews with members of the general staff who expressed their concern and uncertainty about what was going to happen to the Canadian Armed Forces in the future, and how they were going to fulfil their role after all the cuts they had taken in the past. That planted story seemed to indicate, and left Canadians with the impression, that the military was going to share its burden in terms of cuts in order to attack the deficit. That was not the case.
The other story that was planted, was the story about the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Business Council on National Issues attending public meetings and making statements that, yes, business has to take its fair share and bear its share of the burden in terms of cutting the deficit. Some editorialists even suggested that this was a self-sacrificing attitude on the part of the Business Council on National Issues-it would have been the first demonstration of such an attitude-and on the part of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. In fact, nothing was further from the truth. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Business Council on National Issues said that that grants to businesses should be cut or should be converted to repayable loans.
The biggest draw on our resources and on the taxpayer's resources, is not grants to small businesses, the most innovative, employment intensive, product developing businesses in our economy. The biggest drain on the resources of the Dominion of Canada and its exchequer is the drain of the tax expenditures to huge corporations with absolutely no productive results in terms of increased employment or increased economic and indus-

March 7, 1990
The Budget
trial capacity. That has been identified, even by the Nielsen report, as the biggest drain on the resources of this country. Every member on the other side knows that is one series of expenditures that was never touched by the government in this budget. As a result, that group of people, the largest, wealthiest corporations in our society, in our country, do not pay their share. As my colleague from Nickel Belt pointed out, they do not pay any taxes at all in terms of 80,000 to 90,000 of those corporations.
What the people of Canada were looking for in terms of this budget was a little fairness in spreading the burden of that deficit equally among all people in society.
The women's centres in Port Albemi in my riding and in Courtenay will shut their doors on April 30. Courtenay has already shut down now, because the staff does not have time to help women because they are out trying to raise money. In Port Albemi, they are going to be shutting their doors on April 30.
The women's centre in Port Albemi received a generous grant from the federal government of $26,000 a year. Its contribution to fighting the deficit was 100 per cent of that grant.
As my colleague, the leader of the NDP pointed out yesterday, Fletcher Challenge, a major forest company operator in British Columbia, paid zero taxes. What is its contribution to the deficit? As my friend from Nickel Belt pointed out, Hees International, a very profitable corporation, paid zero taxes. What is its contribution to the deficit?
Those were simply planted stories that implied that the defence department was going to be paying its share. It was a planted story that implied that big business was going to be paying its share. Guess what? Those folks did nothing to shoulder their share of the burden of that deficit.
The most cynical scam that was perpetrated on the people of Canada was done by the Minister of Finance between January 11 and January 18 when he dumped the interest rate in Canada by about 29 basis points. I think
he did it on purpose. His purpose in doing that was to panic the currency markets in order to suggest to Canadians that if we reduced interest rates it was going to result in a problem of a declining dollar and serious problems with our currency.
Why did he dump the interest rates at 29 basis points all at one go? If the minister had adopted a more gradualist approach, he could have lowered interest rates by the same amount and more without disturbing the currency markets, without giving them the sense that there was going to be a free fall in interest rates and a free fall in the Canadian dollar which would have created problems with our trading partners, especially in the United States which reacts poorly to a low Canadian dollar. Why did the minister do it? I think it was an attempt to deceive Canadians into believing that interest rates could not be reduced by dumping them all at once instead of taking a more gradualist approach.
Having perpetrated those three scams on the people of Canada, the minister then brought in his budget. It was a very deceptive kind of budget. Having set the stage through those planted stories and through interest rate drive, the minister then tried to imply to Canadians that we were all going to bear the burden equally. But in fact some bore the burden more harshly than others.
I would like to talk for a moment about the budget of the Secretary of State and how it relates in particular to aboriginal organizations. The government has not been too happy with aboriginal organizations over the last little while because they see the impact of federal Conservative policies on their people. Mr. Speaker, you and I know that aboriginal organizations represent some of the poorest of the poor people in Canada, some of the most disenfranchised and powerless people in Canada, people who have a claim under our Constitution for recognition of the role that they played in the development and the history of this country, and they are not recognized in that Constitution. They are people with a legitimate case of unfinished business that needs to be negotiated with this country.
Over the years, the Prime Minister has recognized that, the Parliament of Canada has recognized that, but in this budget the government has put an end to its recognition and support for aboriginal organizations in Canada. Essentially, the government is implementing

the Buffalo Jump provisions of the Nielsen report that was brought down in 1985. The government is saying that native Indians and aboriginal groups are no longer entitled to the support of the Canadian people, that they are going to have to go it on their own, and as far as this government is concerned the policy with respect to aboriginal people is integration, assimilation and cultural annihilation. That is the policy of this government with respect to Indian people.
How do you do it? First of all you wipe out their leadership. In that same Secretary of State's budget that eliminated 100 per cent of some of the women's centre core funding across Canada including two in my riding, the budget of the Assembly of First Nations, the leadership organization of the status Indians of Canada, was wiped out to the tune of 100 per cent. Was there any consultation in advance? No consultation. Was there any discussion in the words of the Associate Minister of Defence in terms of generating new partnerships for fund raising? No discussion about new partnerships. Was there any discussion about getting project moneys, even though you do not have the core funds to operate an office or hire the people? There was no discussion.
The Prime Minister made a promise on April 18,1985, denying the Buffalo Jump document was government policy and saying that he intended to carry on an important relationship with native people and that there would be no cuts in funding without prior consultation. Were any of the promises of the Prime Minister kept? Absolutely not one of those promises was kept. This was a direct attack racially motivated against the native people of Canada.
In the Secretary of State's budget, what is the excuse that the government has for cutting all of the funding of native print media, about $3.4 million? As the clock ticks, that is the interest on our debt. How can these people possibly be accused of contributing to the deficit? With $3.4 million, they employ 108 people who will end up on unemployment insurance as long as it exists and then on welfare. These people have been trained as a result of their journalism experience as journalists, reporters, printers and other technicians involved in that trade.
The Budget
In the native broadcast media as well, people will end up out of work and programming will be cut back. All of the work that these people have done to improve native literacy, to protect native languages and to communicate between native society and Canada's society as a whole in order to reduce racial tensions and increase tolerance between peoples is going to be wiped out with a stroke without a bit of consultation between this government and those groups.
What other possible explanation is there? These people are not the people who are responsible for the deficit. Their pittance of $9 or $10 million contributes next to nothing to the deficit compared to the drain on our resources through tax expenditures to large corporations and the failure to tax profitable corporations. These people are not responsible for the deficit.
The only explanation for the cuts sustained in this budget by native organizations is that this government, for political or other reasons, opposes the native Indian people of Canada. It is attempting to suppress their leadership and ability to communicate with the rest of us Canadians the legitimacy of the grievances they have against us, grievances based on historical claims to this country, claims to self government within our Constitution, and to be treated equally in terms of health care, social programs and their participation in Canadian society. It is a direct attack on native people, in the very same way that this government has taken the attack against women in this country.
The minister mentioned that women's centres had become involved in the provision of social programs. That is a complete and utter falsehood. Absolutely false. I have gone down to the women's centres in my riding and talked to women. They cannot afford, on a $26,000 budget in the case of the Port Albemi Women's Resources Society, to be providing social programs. How can they do it out of $26,000? It does not make sense. It is a silly, inane comment. It is a silly criticism of the role of women's centres.
Those centres provided resources in terms of help and direction. They referred people to social services and they gave women the confidence, the courage and the ability to take advantage of those services.

March 7, 1990
The Budget
This budget is a bad budget. It is not going to deal with the deficit. Canadians are not going to respond to it as something that deals with the deficit, because it does not allow Canadians to shoulder the burden of that deficit fairly. Some people are paying more than others.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to partake in this important debate today on the budget that was introduced by the finance minister just a few short days ago.
This budget is the sixth by the present finance minister. It is a continuation of this government's commitment to our fiscal plan as outlined in the election of 1984.
If we take a look at the election of 1984, and why we came to power and defeated the former Liberal government, it was simply because of the Liberals mismanagement of the economy in the years running up to 1984.
In 1984, when we took office, government spending was completely out of control. No matter how hard or how strongly the opposition members want to argue that point, they cannot argue it convincingly because spending was completely out of control. They were unable and unwilling to manage the economy of this country. The Canadian public ousted the Liberals in 1984 for a very good reason. We have stuck to our agenda of attempting to come to grips with the problems we inherited in 1984. If you will allow me, Mr. Speaker, I will go through some of the problems we inherited and the steps we have taken to rid ourselves of those particular problems. It has not been easy and it will not be easy, but we are going to do it.
If we were to check the record of Liberal government spending over the 15-year period between 1970 and 1985, we would see it reveals that the Liberal Party increased program spending by 18 per cent between 1970 and 1975. It increased spending by 10 per cent in the next five years and, on average, something in the order of 14 per cent per year between 1980 and 1984. There is no economy or country in the world that can sustain that kind of growth in spending. Canada was no exception.
The continued borrowing on the part of the Liberal government got out of control. What happened, Mr. Speaker, as you and everyone in this Chamber can well remember, is that it led to 20 per cent inflation rates. A
20 per cent inflation rate in itself is bad enough, but that was coupled with double digit interest rates.
What happened? The economy went into a tail-spin and continued in that tail-spin. The reason is that the Liberal Party never wants to come to grips with reality. It wants us always to take the sugar-coated pill, to buy our way out of trouble. Fiscal responsibility means absolutely nothing to that party.
For those years that I have mentioned, what that party did was simply the same thing a young, undisciplined child would do if he or she were given a credit card with no sense of responsibility and no sense of what a citizen should do. That is exactly what that party did. It led us down the golden path, only to find at the end of it that there were certain realities we were facing.
Consequently, when we inherited the government in 1984, we had a $200 billion plus debt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, you didn't. It was $170 billion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They can argue that we did not have it. I ask them to talk to anyone who is an accountant, anyone with a sense of responsibility and let them check the books. It was a $200 billion plus debt that we inherited. It does not take a rocket scientist to understand the problem we inherited.
We inherited a $200 billion plus debt at interest rates over 10 per cent. What are we talking about? We are talking about paying interest on a burgeoning debt that was just impossible for the Canadian people to continue to bear.
We took steps immediately to correct that because it is something that we cannot climb out from underneath in a short period of time. We have been in office since 1984, and there is not a Canadian here who will say that we have not taken steps to correct that situation.
The difference between us and members of the Liberal Party is simply that they will take the easy road out. The easy road out is to do absolutely nothing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The
easy road in.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is exactly it, the easy road into power. He could not have said it better, coming from the opposition party itself. The easy way into power to do absolutely nothing, to stand back and let the economy roll on. They stick their heads in the sand, something for

which they are famous and which they have done for the last 20 years, but they do absolutely nothing about it.
What do they want to do? In the final analysis, if they do nothing they are just passing the problem on to their children and their grandchildren. Mr. Speaker, you are old enough to have grandchildren. Maybe I am not and maybe some of the guys doing all the hollering are not. However, believe me, if we had not come to power and if we did not come to grips with it, it would have been their grandchildren who would have inherited this debt.
The figures are alarming. I will go through some of those a little later.
I would like to talk now about our plan for the future. It is one thing to cut expenses, and we have done a good job on that; we have cut expenses. Some of them have been troublesome and difficult to deal with as none of us want to lose services. It is difficult. As the man said, "cut expenditures and cut expenses and cut programs, but don't cut programs that involve my province or involve me as an individual. Lay it on to somebody else".
That is exactly what we are doing here with the GST. I want to try to bring this into the light because part and parcel of this budget is the GST in a sense. We have to come to grips with expenditures, but on the other side we have to come to grips with the revenue side of this thing: the raising of dollars to pay for the services which Canadians want and need.
What is the Liberal Party telling us about the GST? I think most of its comments can be summarized and are reflected in the recent debate between its finance critic, the member for Gloucester, and our finance minister when they met in Alberta on Tuesday evening, I believe it was. What it was, again, was simply false promises. The finance critic's response to the GST on national television when the Minister of Finance asked him "would you scrap the GST" was simply: "Absolutely, absolutely, we absolutely would". Three times he used the word "absolutely" until he had to spend the night in Edmonton and think about what he had said. Then, the first thing on
The Budget
Wednesday morning when they put a television camera in front of him, he took those words back.
Why? It was because some of the Liberal candidates seeking the nomination for the leadership of the party disagree. Why do they disagree? It is because they know that reality is staring us in the face. Reality is staring Canadians in the face, and we have to come to grips with it.
To give an indication of what reality means, yesterday I was speaking to my brother who lives in Fredericton, New Brunswick. He did not have an opportunity to vote for me because obviously he lives in a different riding. I cannot pretend that my brother has always been a Conservative; maybe he is not at all. One thing he said to me yesterday was: "Gee, it must be difficult for you, Greg, when you go back home and you have all these pressing issues on the table". He talked about the difficulty with the budget. He talked about the GST. As far as the GST is concerned I said that what I feel when I go back home now is that Canadians are realizing there are no options there.
We have to give Canadians more credit than what the opposition party is willing to give them as to their level of intelligence. Canadians know that if you spend money you have to be able to pay the bills. That is something members of that party have not realized and will never come to grips with. They are not going to change.
Let me quote from an editorial which appeared in The Edmonton Journal about the debate on the GST between our party and the Liberal Party. It refers to the finance critic and states: "His views expose the empty posturing and promises made by that Liberal Party". That is what it is. The article stated that the finance critic, Mr. Young, entered the debate burdened with all the old Grit spending baggage of the Trudeau years. No one could have expressed it any better.
Members of the Liberal Party talk about what they will do if they form the government.
I will tell you what they will do if they form a government. They will do what they have done every time they have ever formed a government. They allow us as a party to make the tough decisions that have to be made. They then say that they are going to dismantle

March 7, 1990
The Budget
what we have done. We can go through many of those election years where we actually handed the election to that particular party because we were willing to tell the Canadian people the truth, and they did not want to tell them the truth-never have told them the truth.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Always have.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Listen to that. The member himself does not believe it because he has a big smile on his face. He is smiling. He doesn't believe it.
The debt that we inherited in 1984 was a problem for us as a government. No one can deny that we have done a good job in managing that. By the year 1993, if we stay the course-and our party is determined that we are going to stay the course-our borrowing requirements in 1993-94 will be a zero. Our borrowing requirements will be absolutely zero. The Canadian people are demanding that we take action, and we have taken action.
I am proud to stand here and say that I support the government on this budget. I support the finance minister. And the Canadian people support us.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands - Canso):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member seems to blame all problems faced by his government on the previous Liberal government, who have not been in power for six years, I would like to ask him how many more years his government requires to deal with the problems that they have not been able to face over the last six? The debt has doubled, deficits are at the approximate same level as they were when they took office. How many more years does this government need before it will learn how to manage the economy?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was hoping my hon. friend would ask that question. It simply points out that they never listen.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that about two minutes ago I mentioned that by the year 1993-94 our debt requirements or our borrowing requirements will be absolutely zero. That is exactly the point I am attempting to make. The answer to the question, if he can do anything at all in terms of simple grade school arithmetic, is that it is a 10 year period. If we keep them out of office for 10 years we will have accomplished our goal. We will have reduced our borrowing requirements to absolutely zero.
I am going to ask the hon. gentleman to go back to grade school, or at least get his calculator out because I am convinced that my grade four son could come up with the figures he is asking for.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to rise today as the representative for Selkirk to speak on the government's budget of February 20, 1990.
The key to understanding this budget is understanding the debt. Our national debt is $350 billion. It is what we owe the investors who lent the previous government money to help it pay in a small way for the effects of the recession and more so for its runaway program spending which was rising at an annual rate of 12 per cent. When spending begins to exceed revenue so significantly the result is what we have right now, a debt crisis.
Make no mistake, we have to repay this debt. We either do it now or our children will have to foot the bill, with interest. As a father of three children, I do not want them to inherit this burden. You might well ask why we in the Conservative government have not paid off the debt. After all we have raised taxes and have had five years of strong economic growth.
Well, that is a fair and important question. In 1984 the debt was $200 billion. Even though the government was in debt it was still spending more on programs than it was taking in in taxes. It is borrowing more money just to pay the interest on the debt. It is as if you go over your limit on your credit card and you have a cash advance from your credit card to pay your debt on your credit card. It makes no sense to me.
The bottom line was we inherited a government that was $200 billion in debt, borrowing money to pay the interest and spending more on programs than it was taking in in taxes. What have we done about it? We recognized that the first step towards paying off the debt was to eliminate the operating deficit. We had to stop spending more money than we made. We cut spending, we raised taxes and we closed loopholes.
After just two years we eliminated the operating deficit of $16 billion. We have today an operating surplus of $9 billion. Seventy per cent of this $25 billion turnaround is the result of reduction in government spending. Unfortunately, all the time we have been working to eliminate the operating deficit the interest on the original $200 billion has been accumulating. Interest
March 7, 1990

alone on the debt since 1984 has been $120 billion. Eighty per cent of our debt today is a result of the previous government.
Sometimes we are criticized for blaming the previous government for the debt problem. That does not wash. The fact of the matter is we are sitting on a mountain of debt incurred by our predecessors and the facts bear that out. Our opposition is asking us why, after five years, we have been unable to fix the mess they gave us. We, as a government, get enough criticism for the things that we have actually done, never mind getting it in the ear for policies we had no influence over.
I hear complaints from numerous constituents about government spending. Several months ago I polled the views of my constituents on the national deficit. I asked two questions. The first was: "Are the government deficits and the accumulated national debt a serious problem to you? If so, should the government raise taxes? If so, which ones?". Second, "Should the government cut program spending to reduce debt?"
I asked these questions to determine the economic issues that were of the greatest concern for my constituents. I would like to address the concerns raised by the people of Selkirk and to illustrate how this government has responded to their concerns in this budget. Ninety-six per cent of the people who responded stated that the government's deficit and the national debt are of serious concern to them, but 45 per cent said the government should not raise taxes. We as a government have listened to the concerns of Canadians. There are no new taxes in this budget. Of the 55 per cent who said the government should raise taxes, 82 per cent stated that the corporate tax should be raised.
This, in fact, was accomplished in the 1989 budget. A significant amount of revenue will be raised through the large corporation tax, for instance. The changes in taxation to this sector are expected to raise an additional $1 billion.
Sixty-eight per cent of the respondents said no to the federal government reducing transfer payments to the province of Manitoba. Substantial deficit reduction cannot be achieved without affecting transfers to the prov-
The Budget
inces. They are simply too large a part of the federal expenses to be ignored.
In the fiscal year just ending, tax and cash transfers to provincial governments will total more than $35 billion. They have risen at an average annual rate of 6.5 per cent since 1984-85. During the same period spending on federal programs in general has been held to an average annual growth rate of 3.6 per cent, which is below the rate of inflation. Under the budget's expenditure control plan transfers to provinces are expected to grow by about 3 per cent on average over the next two years, roughly the same rate as all the other program spending.
The EPF transfer to Manitoba will be limited to the same per person level as it was in 1989-90 for the next two fiscal years. Equalization transfers, which in Manitoba are more than EPF, are expected to continue to grow with the national economy. This means that they will grow much faster than other federal spending. Growth of social assistance transfers to Manitoba under the Canada Assistance Plan will also be unaffected because the budget exempts provinces which receive equalization from the 5 per cent cap on growth of these payments.
The result of those transfers to Manitoba under the three major programs, which in 1989-90 total $1.7 billion, are expected to rise in the next two fiscal years to $1.8 billion and $1.87 billion respectively.
I am not suggesting that there is no effect on Manitoba.
There is.
The reduction in the rate of growth of transfer payments represents just under 1 per cent of the provincial government's revenue. But I believe the effects can be coped with as federal and provincial efforts are made to ensure that each tax dollar is spent more carefully, and as all Canadians adjust their expectations of what in current circumstances the federal government can be expected to deliver.
Returning to the survey responses, 66 per cent stated that agricultural spending programs should not be reduced. The farmers of Beausejour in my riding of Selkirk will be glad to know that there have been no reductions to any federal government agricultural program. Farm-

The Budget
ers in Manitoba have already received their cheques on the basis of the multi-year disaster benefit program.
The last major point I want to raise is the fallacy that we have not done our part, that the federal government has not cut enough of its own budget.
We have reduced the Public Service by 12,000 person-years. We are governing in the 1990s with 1973 staff levels because we are managing more efficiently. We have reduced the deficit as a percentage of the GNP every year since 1984, from a high of almost 10 per cent to below 4 per cent. We have kept our spending below the rate of inflation every year.
That is a better record than every province and better than even the private sector. However, I would like to make special mention of the government of Manitoba which has been among the leaders in low percentage increases in its program spending.
The federal government has done its part to cut the deficit. We have got the scars and popularity to prove it.
In conclusion, the budget is fair in its demands and promises clear rewards in the form of a healthier economy, greater financial security for all levels of government and for all Canadians. It offers a positive future for our children.
Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands -
Canso): Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate on the second Tory budget since my election. There are many things that can be said about this budget. I would like to address them under the general theme of fiscal management or, more accurately, the lack of it since the government came to power.
The finance minister is approaching his sixth year on the job. The effort that was tabled on February 20 demonstrates the signs of a man who has never learned the fundamentals of the job, or has simply just given up trying.
I was a federal public servant in Ottawa when the finance minister released his agenda paper on November 8, 1984. The paper proclaimed:
The growing public debt has become a severe handicap to economic
progress and the most serious obstacle to economic growth. Continued
high deficits and growing debt will increasingly undermine confidence,
put upward pressure on interest rates and reduce prospects for growth.
Moreover, they increasingly constrain the federal government's ability
to discharge its responsibilities for over-all economic management
and effective economic leadership.
The agenda paper warned of the consequences of the debt if it reached the feared level of 1990-1991 of the $400 billion it projected as its unacceptable scenario. The minister promised strong leadership directed at attacking the national debt and bringing down high deficits.
It is true deficits were unacceptably high in the two or three preceding years as Liberal governments struggled to guide Canadians through the worst economic recession of the post-war era, a recession that was global in scope and which was the culmination of deep-seated inflationary pressures, not the least of which were two major world energy shocks in the 1970s.
Even though world economic conditions were unfavourable for Canada throughout the seventies, annual budgetaiy deficits either in absolute terms or as a percentage of GDP were never as consistently high as during the last five years under this government. The previous Liberal governments before the Tories came to power had begun to turn the economy around and to bring unemployment and inflation down.
Moreover, with world oil prices falling and the U.S. economy experiencing strong growth, this government had the relatively easy task of presiding over a generally buoyant economy due mainly to more favourable trends around the world.
As the Minister of Finance knows, this was the ideal time to bring deficits down to zero, reduce the national debt and to provide room for lower interest rates to prolong the recovery. But what did the Minister of Finance and his colleagues in the government do during this period? They fiddled, flustered, fulminated and raised taxes 31 times, increasing government revenues by over $170 billion over this period.
What happened to the national debt? It just mushroomed. It ballooned. During the last five years and up until the forecast in the 1989 fiscal plan for 1991, the debt grew to some $379 billion-almost the $400 billion the Minister of Finance predicted in his worst case scenario back in November, 1984.
What did the Minister of Finance do in the intervening years? He gave more tax breaks to his corporate buddies while cranking up taxes on ordinary Canadians. He promised expensive toys to the military, such as the nuclear submarines. He promised billions for major
March 7, 1990

energy projects. He promised to maintain the UI program and to invest in a new child care program for all Canadians.
During the last election campaign the Minister of Finance assured Canadians that all these promises were not promises but spending commitments and fully accounted for within the fiscal framework. Then came the election and Canadians were suddenly advised that, no, the cupboard was bare. There was no money for a national child care program. There was no money for the Polar 8 ice-breaker. There was no more money for regional development. ACOA was going to have to be reprofiled. The government would have to bail out of its unemployment insurance program, after being a financial partner in this program for the past 50 years.
We were told that Canadians would have to pay a massive new sales tax, the goods and services tax, which would tag an extra 7 per cent on to the price of virtually everything we buy. This tax was no longer revenue neutral but was designed to fight the minister's new deficit reduction fervour.
Now we have the February 20 budget, the budget of a tired finance minister in a tired government.
Let me read a few choice morsels from this document. "The deficit for this year is on track at $30 billion". That is what this budget document says. The finance minister now regards a $30.5 billion deficit as an accomplishment.
Then the minister stated: "I am proposing a two-year expenditure control program that will affect all areas of government spending with the exception of income support programs for seniors, families and veterans, unemployment insurance, as well as the equalization
The Budget
program and Canada Assistance Plan payments to lower income provinces".
What he then sets out to do in typical Tory fashion is to attack the economically less powerful members of our society-the veterans, native people, students, those he missed in the April, 1989, budget-and to pass off his government deficit problems on the backs of the provinces.
Here is another quote: "Implementing the expenditure control program this year will require the patience and understanding of Canadians". That is the understatement of the century.
Here is the classic capitulation. "The economy is in a period of slower growth. This is not surprising, nor should we try to avoid it".
Higher interest rates and a higher dollar caused by five years of fiscal mismanagement are driving Canada into a recession and we should sit back and enjoy the ride.
Finally, one more quote from the budget: "This is the future we have been building since 1984." This is the budget of a Minister of Finance who has given up and is too proud to admit it. It is an admission of defeat. It is a cryptic call to the Prime Minister for a portfolio change. I urge the Prime Minister, be merciful to your faithful friend and to Canadians; withdraw this budget and give the minister another job.
